events.name: Sports & Active Nutrition Summit Europe 2026
events.description: NutraIngredients' one-day sports and active nutrition conference, followed on 10 and 11 November by its Nutra Healthspan Summit at the same venue. Programme tracks: State of the Market, Fuelling Performance, Reconsidering Recovery, Weight Management; main room the Partnership Forum, breakouts in Affiliation Hubs.

summary.Summary: Nick Morgan (Nutrition Integrated) opened the day by arguing that the principles of sports nutrition have gone further, rather than sports nutrition itself going mainstream, and put three questions to the room: is the category growing beyond the motivations that defined it, is it winning consumers while losing its identity, and is the market growing or are the boundaries just moving [00:00] (photo 31). His three rules were that growth does not guarantee value, relevance does not guarantee ownership, and opportunity does not guarantee advantage [00:00]. The evidence was Starbucks' 15 g protein cold foam (Starbucks say one in seven coffees now carries 15 g of protein), whey protein at historically high prices (WPI at EUR 30.5 a kilogram and WPC80 at EUR 27.6 by July 2026, about fourfold on 2023, on Vesper's index) and the brand responses to it (fewer promotions, 1 kg packs cut to 900 g at the same price, reformulation, "whey hybrids", whey milkshakes, whey plus collagen at 10 g plus 10 g), creatine moving into gummies, chocolate and products for women, and a hydration market with no agreed electrolyte dose [00:00] (photo 4) (photo 6) (photo 18). He showed the scale of competition from Nutrition Integrated's tracking of 16,412 product listings across the US and Europe: 3,448 creatine products, 2,833 magnesium and 2,648 collagen, with branded ingredients in 53% of pre-workouts, 40% of longevity products and 25% of creatine products [00:00], [18:50] (photo 23) (photo 27). He closed on four principles (think beyond the category, stay true to your DNA, choose where to compete, know your right to win) and on "permission to play" and the right to win: everyone has a seat at the table, but not everyone will win [18:50] (photo 32).
summary.Key takeaways:
- Starbucks' protein cold foam (15 g) started in Q4 2025 in America and is now in the UK, Central Europe, Singapore and India; Starbucks say one in seven coffees currently provides 15 g of protein. "A bigger market does not simply mean more of the same market." [00:00]
- Raw whey prices: on Vesper's EU index, WPI rose from about EUR 11 a kilogram in January 2023 to EUR 30.5 by July 2026 and WPC80 from about EUR 7 to EUR 27.6, while WPC35 moved only from about EUR 3 to EUR 4.3; the slide calls it "the strongest period of price inflation on record", with WPC80 and WPI up about fourfold on 2023 and the sharpest acceleration in H1 2026 [00:00] (photo 4).
- Whey protein prices have never been higher and brands are going through a "structural reset", not mitigation: fewer promotions, pack architecture (1 kg to 900 g at the same price), some reformulation, a rush of new whey launches, and a push to sell higher-margin lines instead. Consumer prices per kilogram for priority brands in Europe rose between October 2025 and October 2026 by 13.6% for clear whey (EUR 60.14 to 68.32), 28.0% for HWP/WPI (47.73 to 61.10), 28.8% for whey blends (37.56 to 48.38), 15.0% for whey hybrids (35.64 to 40.97) and 20.8% for WPC (36.66 to 44.29); he said 15 to 25 percent from the stage. He believes protein will "look quite differently in 18 to 20 months" [00:00] (photo 8).
- His mitigation ladder has six rungs: price increases (widespread), reduced promotion (increasingly common) and pack architecture (widely adopted globally) are tactical; reformulation is strategic and brand specific; new products that cut whey reliance and a portfolio shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the "top priority for brands", with the limitations named as a ground-zero revenue base, brand permission and alienating core consumers [00:00] (photo 6).
- Brands "would love to listen to you about some really good solutions": they want to sell more creatine, electrolytes, pre-workout and higher-value vitamins because the margin structure is better than whey [00:00].
- "Whey hybrids" (presented as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost of goods) launched in greater numbers in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes (whey plus milk) and whey plus collagen (typically 10 g plus 10 g, in shakes and clear drinks) are the next pillars; GLP-1 and longevity proteins, yeast, mycelium and air-derived protein are coming through but are still expensive [00:00]. The slide's examples were Bulk Daily Whey Protein ("best value protein"), Myprotein's Impact Whey Protein Milkshake (20 g protein, 2.6 g sugar, 1.2 g fat per 29 g serving), Clean Simple Eats Protein Powder + Collagen and Planta (20 g protein, 24 vitamins and minerals, 1,000 mg BCAAs) (photo 9).
- Six "pillars of innovation" from the price squeeze: whey choice risks confusing consumers; communications react more than they solve; hybrid powders are gaining consistency (dairy plus plant in overt blends); caseinate is the new milkshake; plant protein still needs a taste breakthrough; and the Myprotein x Nero launch signals a race for the next cafe collaboration [00:00] (photo 12).
- Plant protein is not taking the gap: ranges come in and out because they still underdeliver on taste. The winning message is "we're just a really bloody good protein", not "plant"; dairy plus plant hybrids are appearing for the first time and caseinates are gaining with milk volatility [00:00]. His example was Rocka's vegan range: Pro Protein at 24 g protein, 122 kcal, an 83% fava bean and pea blend, EUR 37.99 per 700 g (EUR 1.65 a serve); Natural Protein at 21 g, 112 kcal, 86.6% soy, fava, almond and pea, EUR 29.99 per 600 g (EUR 1.50 a serve); Protein Shake, "the tastiest vegan protein powder", 84% blend, EUR 37.99 per 900 g (EUR 1.27 a serve), plant moving "from an extended product proposition to a simple product attribute" (photo 10).
- The creatine benchmark is Optimum Nutrition's Micronised Creatine Powder: 3 g creatine monohydrate a serve, GBP 14.00 for the 187 g unflavoured tub (25p a serve, EUR 0.33) and GBP 16.00 for 247 g flavoured (29p a serve), fronted by Lauren James, Chelsea and England footballer (photo 13).
- Creatine is now "for all people and for all occasions"; gummies are the fastest-growing format by new launches in the last six months, off a small base, with "lots of conjecture about stability"; "other" formats (liquids, foods, chocolate) grew faster still off a tiny base, and most brands now have a route into broader retail [00:00], [25:59]. The format split of 2,639 creatine products: powder 70.1% (13.1% added in the last six months), capsule 17.0% (8.7%), gummy 8.0% (36.2%), tablet 4.2% (14.4%), effervescent 0.4% (10.0%), other 0.3% (44.4%); 378 products, 14.3% of the total, were added in six months. The examples were Creatonics' "Creatine+ formulated for women" sachet and Sunday Natural's Nutrachoc creatine chocolate (20 pieces at 1,000 mg creatine monohydrate, sweetened with tagatose) (photo 14) (photo 15).
- Hydration: no agreed electrolyte dose (SiS "all five essential", LMNT 1,000 mg sodium, Precision by sweat rate); Liquid IV is the category leader at £1.50 a stick; effervescents are three times cheaper than a stick pack; naturalness (no colours or preservatives, natural sweeteners and flavours, short ingredient lists) is a prerequisite to growth [00:00]. The shelf prices on the slide: Liquid I.V. GBP 1.50 a sachet (GBP 9.00 for 6; GBP 1.00 on Clubcard), Phizz GBP 0.40 a tablet (GBP 8.00 for 20; GBP 0.28 on Clubcard), Evian 750 ml GBP 1.85 single, Red Bull 250 ml GBP 2.10 single, Lucozade Sport 500 ml GBP 1.65 single (photo 16).
- Declared sodium a serve on selected electrolyte powders runs from 38 mg (ViDrate Boost) through 350 mg (SiS Hydro+), 500 mg (Cadence Daily), 570 mg (Liquid I.V. Multiplier) and 750 mg (Hunter & Gather) to 1,000 mg (LMNT); 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes, and 8% of products claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural sodium source. The slide's heading: "there is no optimal formula" [00:00] (photo 18).
- Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday hydration (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior hydration (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance hydration (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).
- Naturalness in ingredient declarations: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours and 43% include stevia; Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition and Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).
- Product counts tracked (US and Europe, 16,412 listings across eight spaces): 3,448 creatine (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), 2,833 magnesium (+15%), 2,648 collagen, 2,153 energy and focus, 1,869 pre-workout, 1,626 sleep and mood, 1,487 electrolyte and 348 longevity (+20% new); he said almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium and over 2,500 collagen from the stage. "Only a few will be really successful", by pulling on format, brand, dose, science and branded solutions [00:00] (photo 23).
- Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%; in creatine most comes from one supplier and "there's a race for those to follow". His slide's nuance: minerals "need to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).
- Longevity products take three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life); Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing was the example [18:50] (photo 29).
- Longevity brands and athlete-backed brands (Sergio Ramos linking sport to longevity through Centenarian: "Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better.") compete for the same consumer with sports nutrition products framed as "live better today"; the competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).
- Brands must think beyond the category (gut, longevity, GLP-1) but stay true to the industry's DNA, choose where to compete and understand the right to win; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].
- The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)
summary.For Vita Actives: Whey margin pressure is the strongest tailwind in the talk for an ingredient supplier: brands are actively looking for higher-margin, non-whey lines and for new protein blends, and he told the room they want to hear solutions [00:00]; his own slide lists a portfolio shift into creatine, energy and fibre as a "top priority for brands" (photo 6). For CreaWin: creatine is his benchmark category, 25% of 3,448 products use a branded ingredient, most of it from one supplier, and he said there is a race to follow [18:50] (photo 27); my reading is that this is exactly the gap a second branded creatine pitches into, with science and story as the differentiators he named. Gummies (8.0% of products, 36.2% added in six months) and food formats are where creatine launches are growing and stability is the open question [00:00] (photo 14); my reading is that a stability story for CreaWin in gummies would land with brands. The ON benchmark sets the consumer price floor at 25p a serve for 3 g (photo 13). For IsoClr: Pea: his point that plant protein must be sold as a very good protein rather than as plant, and that taste is the barrier, fits a clear pea isolate pitched on taste and clarity first (my reading); Rocka's range shows fava and pea blends sold at EUR 1.27 to 1.65 a serve (photo 10). The whey hybrid and whey plus collagen trend shows brands will blend protein sources, including in clear drinks, which opens room for a pea component in clear formats (my reading). For Oxystorm: pre-workout has the highest branded-ingredient penetration, 53%, so it is crowded but receptive to branded actives (photo 27) (my reading). Naturalness and short ingredient lists are a prerequisite across the board [00:00] (photo 24). Relevance high: it is the market-structure and protein-pricing frame for everything else at this event.
summary.Quotes:
- "A really important point here is that a bigger market does not simply mean more of the same market." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]
- "They want to sell higher value vitamins, more pre-workout, more electrolytes, more creatine, because they have a better value chain and margin structure. And so, brands would love to listen to you about some really good solutions that you have." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]
- "We have never seen more whey hybrids launched in the last 12 months than ever before. It is a fundamental product pillar." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]
- "What it really wants to say is we're just a really bloody good protein. That is the ideal. By differentiating yourself as being plant, typically lends people to assume it doesn't taste as good." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]
- "Creatine, which is my benchmark, one in four products uses a branded ingredient. It wouldn't take you a genius to work out where most of that comes from. There's a race for those to follow, by the way." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]
- "The growth is good, and it creates opportunity. You all have a seat at the table, but it doesn't mean to say you're all going to win." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]
- "Demand continues to exceed available WPI and WPC80 production capacity, resulting in the strongest period of price inflation on record." Slide (photo 4)
- "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." Slide (photo 32)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ask Nick Morgan (Nutrition Integrated) for the branded-ingredient penetration data by category and the creatine format split (gummies, "other") behind the slides, and why the format table counts 2,639 creatine products while the tracked-listings slide counts 3,448 [00:00], [18:50] (photo 14) (photo 23).
- "Brett" presents the whey milkshake later in the day; the whey plus collagen talk is Rousselot's (filed as whey-collagen-the-protein-power-couple) [00:00].
- Check the brands Otter heard as "Sonero" (longevity), "Rocker" (plant protein architecture: pro, natural, standard) and "solely" (protein from air), and the Sergio Ramos-backed sports nutrition brand [00:00], [18:50]. The slides give Rocka for the plant range (photo 10) and Centenarian for Sergio Ramos (photo 30); the longevity example on the slide is Cellaro (photo 29), which may be "Sonero" (my reading); the protein-from-air brand is not on a slide.
- Myprotein's coffee collaboration with Nero (on the slide, photo 12) and the Malaysian coffee collaboration he mentioned [00:00].

Whey protein price mitigation
From cyclical volatility to structural reset. The industry response is rapidly evolving beyond tactical pricing mitigation. While immediate actions buy time, long-term resilience and profitability increasingly depend on reformulation, alternative protein architectures (such as plant and hybrid blends), and diversification into non-whey adjacent functional nutrition.
01 / TACTICAL Price Increases. Benefits: Some margin recovery; Simple to implement. Limitations: Price elasticity risks; Retailer pushback; Competitive disadvantage. Observation: Widespread across market.
02 / TACTICAL Reduce Promo. Benefits: Protects base margins; Limits low-margin volume. Limitations: Lower sales velocities; Reduced shelf visibility; Consumer friction. Observation: Increasingly common.
03 / TACTICAL Pack Architecture. Benefits: Lowers absolute price; Retains entry-level buyers. Limitations: Smaller/fewer servings; Unit price inflation risk; Overall volume risk. Observation: Widely adopted globally.
04 / STRATEGIC Reformulation. Benefits: Structural cost reduction; Margin resilience. Limitations: Sensory/taste profile risks; Potential trust issues; Adjacent price volatility. Observation: Brand specific activity.
05 / FUTURE FOCUS New Products. Benefits: Decreases whey reliance; Unlock plant & hybrid. Limitations: Ground zero revenue base; Consumer education; Taste expectations. Observation: Top priority for brands.
06 / FUTURE FOCUS Portfolio Shift. Benefits: Sell other products; Creatine, Energy, Fibre. Limitations: Brand permission; Alienate core consumers; May not replace revenue. Observation: Top priority for brands.
Figure 5. The strategic choices brands are working through in order to mitigate the impact of high whey protein prices. 02. Growth > Value

Plant protein vs just protein
Rocka range. Pro Protein: "Vegan Performance Protein". Higher protein dose (24g) + a slightly higher calorie content (122kcals) to achieve a "smooth, creamy, indulgent taste". 83% plant protein blend [fava bean & pea]. EUR 37.99 per 700g tub [EUR 1.65 per serve].
Natural Protein: "Naturally-flavoured & a monk-fruit sweetened powder". A slightly lower protein dose (21g) & reduced calorie content (112kcals). 86.6% plant protein blend [soy protein isolate, fava bean, almond & pea protein]. EUR 29.99 per 600g tub [EUR 1.50 per serve].
Protein Shake: "The tastiest vegan protein powder". Reflects a similar profile to the Natural formulation yet it doubles down on "shake" terminology. 84% plant protein blend [soy, pea, almond & fava bean protein]. EUR 37.99 per 900g tub [EUR 1.27 per serve].

A difference in electrolyte opinion
HOW BRANDS EXPLAIN THEIR ELECTROLYTES (Approach: Explanation and brand example)
Number & completeness: SiS highlights five essential electrolytes. Number reassures, and the premise of "comprehensive" seems intuitive.
Sweat-loss replacement: Veloforte links minerals to sweat losses, giving electrolytes a clear purpose and reason to choose.
Dose & strength: LMNT promotes a meaningful dose. Explain who it suits, rather than implying that more means better.
Blend, ratio & science: Bulk promotes optimum ratios, communicating why the chosen blend is right for the need.
Personal relevance: Precision matches strengths to sweat losses, helping consumers choose the right product for their needs.
Natural sources & wider benefits: Hunter & Gather uses natural minerals and daily balance, adding reasons to buy beyond the blend.
SIMILAR BREADTH, DIFFERENT DOSES. 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes (footnote 1).
Sodium per serve varies widely. Selected powders, declared sodium (mg/serve): ViDrate Boost 38 mg; SiS Hydro+ 350 mg; Cadence Daily 500 mg; Liquid I.V. Multiplier 570 mg; Hunter & Gather 750 mg; LMNT 1000 mg. Axis 0 to 1200.
Selected products, not the full-category distribution. *8% of products claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural approach to sodium.

Transcribed by Claude from the photo; the photo is the original. Nick Morgan, Nutrition Integrated, SANS Europe, 9 Nov 2026.
--- photo 23 ---
A challenge to cut through the noise
TRACKED PRODUCT LISTINGS | US + EUROPE: 16,412 across eight high-interest nutraceutical spaces.
With thousands of products competing for attention, how does a brand become memorable? FORMAT, BRAND, DOSE, SCIENCE, BRANDED SOLUTIONS (highlighted).
Creatine 3,448 (+10%) | Magnesium 2,833 (+15%) | Collagen 2,648 | Longevity 348 (+20% new)
Energy & Focus 2,153 | Preworkout 1,869 | Sleep & Mood 1,626 | Electrolyte 1,487
Cutting through requires the right combination of levers. Growth callouts represent new-product activity over the latest six-month period.
# It is quite overwhelming when you sit back and think about how many products there are available to consumers in any one category.
# The reality is, only a few will be really successful, and in order to do so they will have to pull on some key levers to differentiate.
Figure 16. A brief snapshot of the number of products available to consumers in a variety of categories | US, Europe. 03. Opportunity > Advantage

files.name: otter-summary.md
files.text:
Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Nick Morgan discusses the evolution of sports nutrition as it moves into the mainstream and explores the resulting market tensions.

## Market Evolution
**Nick** argues that sports nutrition is expanding beyond its original motivations, moving from niche athletic use to everyday consumption. He highlights several key shifts:
*   **Mainstream Integration**: The **Starbucks** protein-infused coffee trend serves as a primary example of sports ingredients entering daily rituals.
*   **Identity Shifts**: As the category grows, there is a risk of losing its core identity while simultaneously winning a broader consumer base.
*   **Expanding Boundaries**: The market is not just growing in volume but is redefining its boundaries through new categories like longevity and gut health.

## Industry Tensions
**Nick** outlines significant challenges regarding value, relevance, and competition within the current landscape.
**Protein Dynamics**
The high cost of whey protein has triggered a structural reset among brands. To manage margins, companies are utilizing several strategies:
*   **Whey Hybrids**: Products that blend whey with cheaper sources like milk, soy, or yeast while still marketing as whey-based.
*   **New Formats**: The rise of "whey milkshakes" and collagen-blended proteins to extend product benefits.
*   **Alternative Sources**: Emerging interest in yeast, mycelium, and even protein made from air.
*   **Cost Management**: Brands are using pack architecture changes (e.g., 900g instead of 1kg) and reformulation to offset costs.

**Competitive Landscape**
The sheer volume of products—including 3,500 creatine products and 2,800 magnesium products—creates massive confusion. **Nick** notes that while opportunity is high, advantage is not guaranteed due to extreme competition.
*   **Hydration**: The market is fragmented between different electrolyte approaches (sodium-focused vs. sweat-rate focused) and formats like stick packs versus cheaper effervescent tablets.
*   **Longevity**: There is a growing intersection between sports performance and aging, exemplified by athletes like **Sergio Ramos** linking sports nutrition to cellular health.

## Strategic Outlook
The presentation concludes by emphasizing that brands must navigate "permission to play" in new territories without losing their DNA.
*   **Differentiation**: Success requires leveraging branded ingredients, science-backed narratives, and unique delivery formats such as gummies or functional foods.
*   **Future Focus**: Companies must prepare for how trends like **GLP-1** and the microbiome will influence consumer behavior through 2027.

Action items: none returned.

takeaways.text: Starbucks' protein cold foam (15 g) started in Q4 2025 in America and is now in the UK, Central Europe, Singapore and India; Starbucks say one in seven coffees currently provides 15 g of protein. "A bigger market does not simply mean more of the same market." [00:00]

Raw whey prices: on Vesper's EU index, WPI rose from about EUR 11 a kilogram in January 2023 to EUR 30.5 by July 2026 and WPC80 from about EUR 7 to EUR 27.6, while WPC35 moved only from about EUR 3 to EUR 4.3; the slide calls it "the strongest period of price inflation on record", with WPC80 and WPI up about fourfold on 2023 and the sharpest acceleration in H1 2026 [00:00] (photo 4).

Whey protein prices have never been higher and brands are going through a "structural reset", not mitigation: fewer promotions, pack architecture (1 kg to 900 g at the same price), some reformulation, a rush of new whey launches, and a push to sell higher-margin lines instead. Consumer prices per kilogram for priority brands in Europe rose between October 2025 and October 2026 by 13.6% for clear whey (EUR 60.14 to 68.32), 28.0% for HWP/WPI (47.73 to 61.10), 28.8% for whey blends (37.56 to 48.38), 15.0% for whey hybrids (35.64 to 40.97) and 20.8% for WPC (36.66 to 44.29); he said 15 to 25 percent from the stage. He believes protein will "look quite differently in 18 to 20 months" [00:00] (photo 8).

His mitigation ladder has six rungs: price increases (widespread), reduced promotion (increasingly common) and pack architecture (widely adopted globally) are tactical; reformulation is strategic and brand specific; new products that cut whey reliance and a portfolio shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the "top priority for brands", with the limitations named as a ground-zero revenue base, brand permission and alienating core consumers [00:00] (photo 6).

Brands "would love to listen to you about some really good solutions": they want to sell more creatine, electrolytes, pre-workout and higher-value vitamins because the margin structure is better than whey [00:00].

"Whey hybrids" (presented as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost of goods) launched in greater numbers in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes (whey plus milk) and whey plus collagen (typically 10 g plus 10 g, in shakes and clear drinks) are the next pillars; GLP-1 and longevity proteins, yeast, mycelium and air-derived protein are coming through but are still expensive [00:00]. The slide's examples were Bulk Daily Whey Protein ("best value protein"), Myprotein's Impact Whey Protein Milkshake (20 g protein, 2.6 g sugar, 1.2 g fat per 29 g serving), Clean Simple Eats Protein Powder + Collagen and Planta (20 g protein, 24 vitamins and minerals, 1,000 mg BCAAs) (photo 9).

Six "pillars of innovation" from the price squeeze: whey choice risks confusing consumers; communications react more than they solve; hybrid powders are gaining consistency (dairy plus plant in overt blends); caseinate is the new milkshake; plant protein still needs a taste breakthrough; and the Myprotein x Nero launch signals a race for the next cafe collaboration [00:00] (photo 12).

Plant protein is not taking the gap: ranges come in and out because they still underdeliver on taste. The winning message is "we're just a really bloody good protein", not "plant"; dairy plus plant hybrids are appearing for the first time and caseinates are gaining with milk volatility [00:00]. His example was Rocka's vegan range: Pro Protein at 24 g protein, 122 kcal, an 83% fava bean and pea blend, EUR 37.99 per 700 g (EUR 1.65 a serve); Natural Protein at 21 g, 112 kcal, 86.6% soy, fava, almond and pea, EUR 29.99 per 600 g (EUR 1.50 a serve); Protein Shake, "the tastiest vegan protein powder", 84% blend, EUR 37.99 per 900 g (EUR 1.27 a serve), plant moving "from an extended product proposition to a simple product attribute" (photo 10).

The creatine benchmark is Optimum Nutrition's Micronised Creatine Powder: 3 g creatine monohydrate a serve, GBP 14.00 for the 187 g unflavoured tub (25p a serve, EUR 0.33) and GBP 16.00 for 247 g flavoured (29p a serve), fronted by Lauren James, Chelsea and England footballer (photo 13).

Creatine is now "for all people and for all occasions"; gummies are the fastest-growing format by new launches in the last six months, off a small base, with "lots of conjecture about stability"; "other" formats (liquids, foods, chocolate) grew faster still off a tiny base, and most brands now have a route into broader retail [00:00], [25:59]. The format split of 2,639 creatine products: powder 70.1% (13.1% added in the last six months), capsule 17.0% (8.7%), gummy 8.0% (36.2%), tablet 4.2% (14.4%), effervescent 0.4% (10.0%), other 0.3% (44.4%); 378 products, 14.3% of the total, were added in six months. The examples were Creatonics' "Creatine+ formulated for women" sachet and Sunday Natural's Nutrachoc creatine chocolate (20 pieces at 1,000 mg creatine monohydrate, sweetened with tagatose) (photo 14) (photo 15).

Hydration: no agreed electrolyte dose (SiS "all five essential", LMNT 1,000 mg sodium, Precision by sweat rate); Liquid IV is the category leader at £1.50 a stick; effervescents are three times cheaper than a stick pack; naturalness (no colours or preservatives, natural sweeteners and flavours, short ingredient lists) is a prerequisite to growth [00:00]. The shelf prices on the slide: Liquid I.V. GBP 1.50 a sachet (GBP 9.00 for 6; GBP 1.00 on Clubcard), Phizz GBP 0.40 a tablet (GBP 8.00 for 20; GBP 0.28 on Clubcard), Evian 750 ml GBP 1.85 single, Red Bull 250 ml GBP 2.10 single, Lucozade Sport 500 ml GBP 1.65 single (photo 16).

Declared sodium a serve on selected electrolyte powders runs from 38 mg (ViDrate Boost) through 350 mg (SiS Hydro+), 500 mg (Cadence Daily), 570 mg (Liquid I.V. Multiplier) and 750 mg (Hunter & Gather) to 1,000 mg (LMNT); 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes, and 8% of products claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural sodium source. The slide's heading: "there is no optimal formula" [00:00] (photo 18).

Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday hydration (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior hydration (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance hydration (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).

Naturalness in ingredient declarations: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours and 43% include stevia; Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition and Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).

Product counts tracked (US and Europe, 16,412 listings across eight spaces): 3,448 creatine (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), 2,833 magnesium (+15%), 2,648 collagen, 2,153 energy and focus, 1,869 pre-workout, 1,626 sleep and mood, 1,487 electrolyte and 348 longevity (+20% new); he said almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium and over 2,500 collagen from the stage. "Only a few will be really successful", by pulling on format, brand, dose, science and branded solutions [00:00] (photo 23).

Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%; in creatine most comes from one supplier and "there's a race for those to follow". His slide's nuance: minerals "need to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).

Longevity products take three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life); Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing was the example [18:50] (photo 29).

Longevity brands and athlete-backed brands (Sergio Ramos linking sport to longevity through Centenarian: "Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better.") compete for the same consumer with sports nutrition products framed as "live better today"; the competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).

Brands must think beyond the category (gut, longevity, GLP-1) but stay true to the industry's DNA, choose where to compete and understand the right to win; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].

The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)

sessions.transcript:
# Unfiltered: An Insider's View of the Whey Protein Market: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Alan Johnstone - SNS - whey pricing", https://otter.ai/u/3wuSdbgu4ue-m20dOaERZG2gsKY, recorded 9 Nov 2026 09:36, 17m 15s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: To deal with it, we've got Alan Johnston, owner of Nutrilution.
[00:16] Speaker 2: I'm going to talk about wafers here. For those who don't know me, I've spent most of the last decades selling whey protein. First at Sarawak International, and then more recently at Arla Foods Ingredients. And so, hopefully, I'm qualified to talk about this. The purpose, really, of this presentation is to give you a better understanding of what happens in the supply chain for whey protein. We're fairly familiar with the consumer side, and that's with the intention that you can understand the restrictions on whey protein manufacturers, but also you can understand some of the decisions they might make over the next few years. Nutrition, as Nikki says, is my new business. We also sell nutritional ingredients, mostly more niche, higher value ingredients, but we can also help buyers with sourcing strategy for whey proteins and dairy proteins generally, especially if you're looking to set up cross continental supply chains. So, if that sounds interesting, then do talk to me afterwards. This slide illustrates nicely why you want this on the agenda. So WPI is the top line on the graph here, rising from around seven euros a kilogram back in 2023, all the way up to over 30 euros per kilogram earlier this year, with very little respite in that curve for buyers. WPCAT actually pretty stable, and I would argue quite good value for most of that time, until earlier this year when the price rocketed from 12 euros per kilogram all the way up to 28 in the space for about six weeks, and it was that sudden increase that put so much pressure on brands and the industry, partly because of the speed, because of course they have no time at all to react, and partly because businesses had already switched their sourcing away from WPI and into WPC80, and that meant that the WPC80 price was more of an existential risk for brands, as opposed to the WPI price, which was more of a break on the Profitability. So we're going to have a little look at why that's happened. Really quick on demand. Nick's covered all of this really, but and traditional sports nutrition grown extremely fast. Urine monitor staying 10% a year. I think most people I know see that as a big underestimate. Probably growing faster than that, GLP-1 again, no secret here. You've got a huge number of adults taking this and spending a lot more money on protein supplements than they had previously. And of course, these are people who weren't necessarily in the gym before, so they probably weren't buying protein supplements before. And this is incremental demand. That's plus protein more mainstream. I've also used the Starbucks example. You could choose Papa John's pizza. You could choose Dunkin' Donuts. It's just just everywhere. And then I've plucked out Clearway as a sub trend. Now, partly because it didn't really exist five years ago, so this is now one of the fastest selling parts of the category, and partly because it is almost all whey, so it has a disproportionate effect on the supply chain for whey proteins. Most of these trends would support all protein sources, and they especially source whey protein because, for most purposes, whey protein is the best protein source. It's nutritionally superior in terms of muscle protein synthesis. Don't mind a debate on whether your average consumer really benefits much from that. You know they probably don't. And in fact, certainly the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source. I think what people always care about is taste and texture. And whey protein is delicious. It is light. It's smooth. It mixes easily. It's just far easier for a business to create a good-tasting whey protein product with whey than it is with most of the alternative protein sources. Hence the surge in demand. Moving to supply, starting the bottom left here, kind of the composition of milk. want to call out that only 0.6 liquid milk is whey protein, and that's important to understand the production process, but also the decisions that whey protein producers take. Because of course, a high whey protein price doesn't necessarily make for a happy dairy farming. You're also going to be able to sell and get value for all of these other elements of the liquid milk as well. In order to get whey protein from that, you start by making cheese. You don't have to. There are other ways of whey protein. Life are the most common. Start with cheese production, and the cheese keeps the casein protein and it keeps most of the fat, and then you end up with liquid whey, which is around 12% protein by dry matter. From there, if you want to get to WPCA, so you go through ultrafiltration, so you're filtering off the minerals, you're filtering off a lot of lactose, like that. But if you want to go to WPR, you go through microfiltration, another production process, and that is where you filter off the remaining fats. But unfortunately, with that fat, you also lose quite a lot of your protein. Then, if you want to add even more value, you want to go to clear whey or you want to go to hydrolyzed whey protein, then you go through yet another production process. And it's these production processes that are one of the first bottlenecks for whey protein supply. These factories are phenomenally expensive, and they take a long time to build. So, if you're a whey protein producer, you're making really big bets a long way in advance, and then you've got to be really confident of your business case in order to do that. And a huge part of your business case is: Can you source enough whey to fill that factory up? So this is the second bottleneck, arguably the most important one, which is that cheese production is only growing around one and a half percent a year, and that means that liquid whey production is only growing around one and a half percent a year. You can, of course, source whey protein from other areas, so you can try and find a cheese factory that wasn't already selling it. You could take whey away from another whey derivative like sweet whey powder or WPC 35, and businesses are doing that. But there's a limit to how much you can do that. Ultimately, you come up against this bottleneck. It's probably the most important conclusion from the presentation already, really, which is that cheese is only growing one and a half percent a year, whereas waferaging demand is growing whatever figure we choose over over 10%. Byproducts are then another limitation on how fast this can grow because you can't only sell the wafers; you've got to sell the byproducts as well. If you're making WPC 80, you're only left with permeate and lactose, which fairly easy to get rid of. If you're making WPI, you've also then got to sell this fatty protein stream, and these byproducts complicate the business cases because if you think that whey protein manufacturers are essentially competing to buy what limited liquid whey is available, the people who can afford to pay the most for the liquid whey are the businesses that can add the most value to them, and that's not just the protein itself; it's also all these byproducts. So, in the way that's played out over the last five years, looks a bit like this. So, you've got total whey protein supply growing just under 5%. Okay, go. So you can see that there's clearly whey being reprioritized away from lower value derivatives into high protein. Within that, then you've got WPI growing a lot faster than WPC8. If you think back to that first graph I showed you with the WPI graph rising higher and earlier, you can understand why producers have prioritized WPI manufacturing capacity. Of course, that's come at the expense of WPC 80 because you can funnel as much weight as you possibly can into WPI production, which it also helps to explain why WPC80 was so undersupplied earlier this year. You might ask, well, if WPI has been growing 15% year on year, why was it so expensive? It's partly because, of course, demand's been growing so fast. It's also because I mentioned the Clearway trend earlier, and a lot of that WPI chunk is now Clearway, and it wasn't five years ago. Estimates vary on what percentage of the WPI market is Clearway. I've used 25% here, which is right at the top of the estimate range. It's probably a little bit below that, but it illustrates that actually the the instant WPI, the normal WPI that you're used to using in the past has been growing much more slowly, more like eight and a half percent a year, and that is below the underlying category level. Looking to the future, so on the left there you've got American manufacturing increases over the next couple of years. This is quite good data. Each one of those little blocks represents a different supplier, so it's quite granular and should be fairly accurate. On the right, I've got European production increases. I've got a lot less detail here, so I've got some names. What they're going to be making. In fact, that's not even an exhaustive list. There's a few manufacturers in Eastern Europe that just can't really get information out of, but the headline is you'd expect WPI to be growing around between seven and 11% a year, WPC 80 a bit slower, four to 7% a year, but both of those figures can't be at the upper estimate. So if WPI is growing 11% a year, then WPC 80 has to be more like four because there's not enough whey. So, with both those figures being relatively modest, you'd argue below the underlying demand for protein. Should we just expect whey protein to become ever more expensive over time? Well, not necessarily, because you've also got a lot of behavior in here. I've used the COVID period here to illustrate a point. It's quite an extreme period, of course, but it does a good job of making this point. If we looked at that graph, you'd expect either supply or demand or both to have been absolutely all over the place. Of course, in reality, they weren't. Both are growing, but they're just growing at different rates. What's really going on here is when COVID hit, buyers stopped buying, which is a fair enough response to uncertainty. So of course the stock levels depleted, and consumers keep buying whey protein products, and they keep probably buying them faster than ever. But at the same time, the supply chain starts to break down. So you've got truck drivers not able to drive. You've got container ships getting stuck at port, and the logistics network just can't keep up with these orders. So if you're a buyer, you're not only trying to replenish the stock that you depleted, you're not only trying to meet increased consumer demand, you're also trying to build extra stocks to allow for a longer lead time. If your lead time has gone from three months to six months, then you need a lot more stock. And because of that, production then can't keep up. So if you're a whey protein supplier, you can't meet all of this extra demand in a short period of time. And so now buyers are competing to be the ones to buy available whey proteins, which means the price goes up. Because the price goes up, buyers are incentivised to buy as early as possible to get the best price. That adds even more to short-term demand, so the price goes up again, and you're into this this vicious cycle. The opposite is also true. So then, looking forward to a time when truck drivers are back on the roads, container ships moving again. All of this, all of these orders, all of this, this demand starts to arrive at warehouses. So inventories grow, and lead times are now shorter. Maybe in the meantime, businesses have taken steps to reduce their usage because of the prices. So they've increased consumer pricing. They've reformulated. They've reduced pack sizes, and now buyers are sitting on quite a lot of stock that they don't really need. So they might say, "Well, I can afford not to buy for a month or two months or whatever it is." Now the stock's growing at the producer level, which means that we're competing to sell. That pushes the price down because the price is falling. Now buyers want to wait as long as they possibly can before they arrive. That pushes demand down even further. Then again, you're back into this this flywheel, and that's a really good example of where we are now. So over the last few weeks, WPC80 has been falling pretty hard. WPI still expensive, but definitely correcting. And this is a direct response to pricing getting so high so fast earlier in the year. Brands have taken all these steps to reduce their usage. In the meantime, you've got a few new factories in commissions in America. So finally, factories that were were probably set in motion three or four years ago when these prices started to go up are finally coming to production, and then there's enough stock to go around so buyers can stock up, and and now they don't need all this extra inventory. So WPAT80 prices is coming down fast. On the other hand, all of the alternatives for things you can do with your whey are expensive. So WPI is still expensive, even WPC 35 is expensive. Even sweet whey powder is now quite a good product to manufacture if you're a producer. So they've got options for what to do with their whey, and that means you'd expect to see WPC 80 production reduce probably quite sharply. Well, right now, but then in the next couple of months as well. Added to that, the alternative proteins that brands have substituted into their formulations are going up in price. So I've used MPC 85 here. You know, you could pick MPI, you can pick caseins, you can pick plant proteins. Really, those two lines, the yellow and the blue line, should never meet. WPC80 should always be more expensive than milk protein. Of course, markets do this. You know the quote from Keane saying that markets can remain irrational for longer than you can remain solvent, so it's it's worth considering that you know just because those lines touch doesn't mean they suddenly bounce away from each other, but it can't go on forever. You'd expect at some stage these these things to correct. So then, looking a little bit ahead, I've used here a deliberately vague graph, so that line is a bit of a blend of WPC80 and WPI price over the last few years, taking all the pricing off, taking most of the timings off because, as I say, it's impossible to be precise with these things. But the way I see the market is, you've got the whey protein price over time rising because demand for proteins, we saw as these many drivers, it's pretty strong. Then you've got a limitation in terms of the speed of liquid whey production. So the price goes up over time, but then the actual price can get quite a long way from what we might consider a balanced price. And you definitely argue that WPCAD did that recently. When it does that, you get these overcorrections driven by the behaviors we just looked at. But then, at some stage, it always gets dragged back towards that, towards that macro trend. That's probably not especially useful for you because, of course, no one knows what a balanced price should be. No one knows how far away the actual price can get before it starts to get dragged back in line. So my advice, as my conclusion for the the presentation, pretty simple. I think don't try to be too clever with your weight rating volume. If you try and buy right at the bottom of the market and you miss it, then you're left trying to replenish stocks when the price is going up, and that's the worst possible time to be doing it. So, if the price that you're paying right now allows you to make money as a business, then keep buying, keep your inventory steady as you can, and then you won't get caught out. But then also realize that whey protein will be expensive. It should be expensive. It's the best protein source for so many uses. It's got a structural supply restriction, and the amount of protein is not really going away. So, if your business can't cope with the sort of supplies we've seen earlier this year, then you need to change something in your business model. All right, I'm done. Time for some questions.
[17:01] Speaker 1: Any questions from the floor at all? I haven't seen any come in on Slido. So brilliant. I think, in the interest of time, we'll move straight on to the panel. But thank you so much, Alan. That was really useful.

summary.Summary: Alan Johnstone (owner of Nutrilution, formerly selling whey at Arla Foods Ingredients) explained the supply chain behind this year's whey prices [00:16]. On Vesper's EU index WPI rose from a trough of about EUR 7 a kilogram in 2023 to EUR 32.00 on 25 August 2026, and WPC80, up roughly sixfold since 2020, jumped from about 12 euros to 28 in about six weeks, which hurt more because brands had already switched into WPC80 [00:16] (photo 2) (photo 16). Demand is growing at over 10% a year (sports nutrition, GLP-1 users, mainstream protein, clear whey, which is almost all WPI), while liquid whey only grows with cheese production at about 1.5% a year, and filtration plants are expensive and slow to build [00:16] (photo 7). Over five years producers grew WPI at 15.0% a year (80,494 t in 2020 to 161,800 t in 2025) and WPC80 at 1.5% (334,000 t to 360,000 t); new capacity suggests WPI at 7 to 11% and WPC80 at 4 to 7% a year to 2030, but not both at the top [00:16] (photo 8) (photo 11). Prices overshoot in both directions on buyer behaviour, and between 25 August and 4 November 2026 WPC80 fell 40.7% to EUR 16.00 a kilogram and WPI 20.3% to EUR 25.50, while MPC85 rose 13.5% to EUR 15.80 and met WPC80 [00:16] (photo 18). His advice: do not try to time the bottom, keep buying steadily if the price lets you make money, and accept that whey "will be expensive. It should be expensive" [00:16] (photo 20).
summary.Key takeaways:
- WPI went from around 7 euros a kilogram in 2023 to over 30 euros earlier this year; WPC80 held around 12 euros, then rocketed to 28 in about six weeks. WPC80 was the existential risk for brands because they had already moved their sourcing into it [00:16]. The slide puts WPI near EUR 32 a kilogram at the summer record and WPC80 up roughly sixfold since 2020, both "now correcting"; its chart (Vesper, EU monthly, December 2019 to October 2026) shows WPC80 at about EUR 5 in 2020 and 2023, peaking about EUR 12 in 2022 and about EUR 26 to 27 in mid 2026, and WPI at about EUR 8 in 2020, EUR 18 in 2022, EUR 7 in 2023 and about EUR 31 in mid 2026 (photo 2).
- Demand drivers: traditional sports nutrition at 10% a year on Euromonitor, which he thinks is a big underestimate; GLP-1 users as incremental demand; protein going mainstream (Starbucks, Papa John's, Dunkin'); clear whey, which barely existed five years ago, is one of the fastest-selling parts of the category and is almost all whey [00:16]. The slide's figures: the 2024 global sports nutrition market splits 48% protein powders, 26% protein bars, 17% non-protein and 9% protein RTD, growing 8 to 10% a year; clear whey SKUs are up 35% year on year; 12% of US adults take a GLP-1 medication, with protein spend up 20% (KFF 2025, BCG 2026); Starbucks' protein drinks carry 15 to 36 g (photo 3).
- Whey wins on taste and texture, not nutrition: "the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source." It is far easier to make a good-tasting product with whey than with most alternatives [00:16].
- Supply: only 0.6% of liquid milk is whey protein (the rest by weight: water 87.3%, lactose 4.7%, fat 3.9%, casein 2.8%, minerals 0.7%); whey comes from cheese, and cheese production grows about 1.5% a year, so liquid whey does too, against demand growing over 10%. This is his most important conclusion [00:16] (photo 4) (photo 7).
- The route from milk: cheese keeps the casein and fat; liquid whey goes through ultrafiltration and drying to WPC (35 to 80% protein), microfiltration or ion exchange to WPI (90% or more), then acidification or hydrolysis to clear or hydrolysed WPI; each step is a plant, and sweet whey powder (about 12% protein), permeate, lactose, demineralised whey (D70, D90, for infant nutrition) and whey cream are the other outlets for the same whey [00:16] (photo 4).
- Factories are the first bottleneck ("phenomenally expensive" and slow to build; the slide: "CAPEX intensive, less flexible than people expect, takes years to start commercial production"); liquid whey is the second; byproducts are the third, "a major influencer of producer value", and WPI producers must also sell a fatty protein stream [00:16] (photo 6) (photo 7).
- Over five years total whey protein supply grew just under 5% a year: global WPC80 plus WPI production rose 26%, from 414,494 t in 2020 to 521,800 t in 2025 (a 4.7% CAGR); WPI grew 15.0% a year (80,494 t to 161,800 t) at the expense of WPC80 at 1.5% (334,000 t to 360,000 t), which explains why WPC80 was undersupplied this year. Clear whey may be up to 25% of WPI (top of the estimate range; 40,450 t of the 161,800 t in 2025); ordinary instant WPI grew 8.6% a year, below the category [00:16] (photo 8) (photo 9).
- New capacity: WPI expected to grow 7 to 11% a year, WPC80 4 to 7% (CAGR 2025 to 2030), but if WPI is at 11, WPC80 has to be more like 4 because there is not enough whey. Both are below underlying demand [00:16] (photo 11).
- The capacity list: announced US additions (McCully Consulting, approximate) of 24,400 t of WPC80 and 7,500 t of WPI in 2026, 41,600 t and 20,300 t in 2027, 45,900 t and 22,900 t in 2028; in the UK, EU and Oceania, FrieslandCampina (WPI expansion), Fonterra (various speciality) and Polmlek (WPC and WPI) in 2026, Tirlan (WPC, WPI and clear) and Liprovit (WPI) in 2027, and Arla's mozzarella plant in 2028. He said the European list is not exhaustive, with some Eastern European producers he could not get information from [00:16] (photo 11).
- Prices overshoot on behaviour, in both directions (the COVID example): buyers stock up when prices rise and sit out when they fall. The slide's cycle: longer lead times, inventory, demand rises, buyers compete for available material, prices rise, incentive to buy early, demand rises again, with the brand and consumer response feeding back into demand; the 2022 peak was logistics freeing up and buyers destocking, the 2023 trough buyers waiting as long as possible with stocks too low [00:16] (photo 13) (photo 15).
- Now: WPC80 "has been falling pretty hard", WPI "still expensive, but definitely correcting"; new US factories set in motion three or four years ago are commissioning; producers have better uses for whey (WPI, WPC35, sweet whey powder), so WPC80 production should fall; MPC85 and other substitutes are rising and WPC80 and milk protein lines "should never meet" [00:16]. The weekly Vesper figures: between 25 August and 4 November 2026 WPC80 fell 40.7%, from EUR 27.00 to EUR 16.00 a kilogram, WPI fell 20.3%, from EUR 32.00 to EUR 25.50, and MPC85 rose 13.5%, from EUR 13.92 to EUR 15.80, meeting WPC80 at about EUR 16 on 4 November (photo 16) (photo 18).
- The MPC85 line: brands substituted MPC85 (or MPI, caseins, plant proteins) into formulations, so those prices are rising while WPC80 falls; he quoted Keynes on markets staying irrational longer than you can stay solvent, so the lines touching does not mean they bounce apart at once, "but it can't go on forever" [00:16] (photo 18).
- What decides the next move, from the slide: for WPC80 the bullish forces are strong other derivatives, rising alternatives and long-term protein demand, the bearish ones high inventories, powerful momentum and demand destruction; for WPI, bullish are its smaller share of brand costs, healthy inventories on both sides and being harder to replace, bearish are demand destruction and production increases due (photo 16).
- Where prices go: "structurally rising but volatile"; the correction is under way and "may overshoot below trend... then demand pulls it back up". The schematic averages EU WPC80 and WPI (Vesper, monthly to October 2026) and the slide says the trend and forward path are "directional, not a forecast" [00:16] (photo 19).
- Advice: do not try to be too clever with volume; buy steadily if the price works; whey will be and should be expensive; a business that cannot cope with this year's prices needs to change its model [00:16]. The three closing takeaways on the slide: "Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." (photo 20)
- Nutrilution also sells niche, higher-value ingredients and advises buyers on whey and dairy protein sourcing, including cross-continental supply chains [00:16].
summary.For Vita Actives: The structural case for non-dairy protein is made by a whey insider: cheese grows 1.5% a year and demand over 10%, and he expects whey to stay expensive [00:16] (photo 7) (photo 20). For IsoClr: Pea, my reading is that this is the opening, but he also set the bar: mainstream consumers care about taste and texture, not source, and whey is the easiest protein to make taste good, so a clear pea isolate has to win on taste and clarity before it wins on supply. Clear whey is almost all WPI, is a quarter of all isolate (40,450 t in 2025) and is where the squeeze is tightest; a clear pea isolate is positioned exactly there (photo 9) (my reading). The next few months are a window: WPC80 fell 40.7% in ten weeks, MPC85 rose 13.5% to meet it, and brands have just reformulated, so they are reviewing formulations and open to blends (photo 18); my reading is that this is the moment to be in front of formulators with pea, before WPC80 settles. Nick Morgan's observation that brands want higher-margin non-protein lines applies here too: CreaWin and Oxystorm are the lines brands want to grow while whey margins are thin (my reading). Nutrilution is a potential partner or competitor in niche ingredients and sourcing advice. Relevance high: protein market structure and pricing.

- "Cheese is only growing one and a half percent a year, whereas waferaging demand is growing whatever figure we choose over over 10%." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "Certainly the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source. I think what people always care about is taste and texture. And whey protein is delicious." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "If WPI is growing 11% a year, then WPC 80 has to be more like four because there's not enough whey." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "So over the last few weeks, WPC80 has been falling pretty hard. WPI still expensive, but definitely correcting." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "Whey protein will be expensive. It should be expensive. It's the best protein source for so many uses. It's got a structural supply restriction, and the amount of protein is not really going away." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "WPI is the growth engine. About a quarter of today's isolate is now Clear WPI, a category that barely existed in 2020." Slide (photo 9)
- "Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." Slide (photo 20)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Talk to Alan Johnstone (Nutrilution) about the WPI/WPC80 price series and the US and European capacity lists he showed; he invited conversations on sourcing strategy [00:16] (photo 11) (photo 18).
- Cross-reference with Rousselot's WPC80 figure of 5.7k a tonne in 2023 to almost 32k in 2026 (whey-collagen-the-protein-power-couple); his Vesper series has WPC80 at about EUR 5 in 2023 and EUR 27.00 on 25 August 2026 (photo 2) (photo 16).
- Check the Euromonitor 10% a year sports nutrition growth figure he cited; the slide says 8 to 10% year on year (photo 3) [00:16].
- The slides credit Vesper (VPI, EU prices) for the price series and McCully Consulting for the US capacity data (photo 2) (photo 11).

Transcribed by Claude from the photo; the photo is the original. Alan Johnstone, Nutrilution, SANS Europe, 9 Nov 2026.
--- photo 4 ---
How whey protein is made, and why there's so little of it (slide 4)
The production journey: from raw milk to refined whey protein. Raw milk (~3.4% protein) -> coagulation (rennet) -> Cheese (the primary product) -> whey drained off -> Liquid whey (co-product of cheese) -> ultrafiltration + drying -> WPC (35-80% protein) -> microfiltration / ion exchange -> WPI (>=90% protein) -> acidify or hydrolyse -> Clear / Hydrolysed WPI (>=90%, refined).
What's in milk (by weight): Water 87.3%; Lactose 4.7%; Fat 3.9%; Casein 2.8%; Minerals 0.7%; Whey 0.6% (whey protein).
Other Whey Derivatives. Beyond protein, there are other options and by-products for producers: Sweet whey powder (~12% protein); Whey permeate (lactose + minerals); Lactose (purified milk sugar); Demineralised whey (D70 / D90, infant nutrition); Procream / WFC (whey cream / fat).
Source: typical cow's-milk composition & dairy processing, indicative industry figures.

files.text:
Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Alan Johnstone provides an analysis of the whey protein supply chain, explaining recent price volatility and long-term market drivers.

## Market Drivers
**Demand Trends**
The surge in demand is driven by several factors:
* Traditional sports nutrition growing at approximately 10% annually.
* Increased consumption due to **GLP-1** medications.
* The rise of "Clear Whey" products, which disproportionately utilize **WPI**.
* General mainstreaming of protein through brands like **Starbucks**, **Papa John's**, and **Dunkin' Donuts**.

**Supply Constraints**
Supply is limited by a fundamental mismatch between production and demand:
* Cheese production (the primary source of liquid whey) grows at only 1.5% per year.
* Protein demand is growing significantly faster than the available liquid whey supply.
* High capital expenditure requirements and long lead times for building new filtration factories create processing bottlenecks.

## Pricing Dynamics
**Volatility Cycles**
**Alan** describes a "vicious cycle" regarding pricing:
1. Supply chain disruptions or sudden demand spikes cause prices to rise.
2. Buyers respond by increasing inventory to mitigate risk, further driving up short-term demand and prices.
3. Conversely, when prices peak, brands reformulate or reduce usage, eventually leading to excess inventory and falling prices.

**Current Status**
Earlier this year, **WPC80** saw a massive price spike from 12 euros to 28 euros per kilogram in six weeks due to manufacturers prioritizing higher-value **WPI**. Currently, **WPC80** prices are correcting downward as new American manufacturing capacity comes online and brands reduce usage through reformulation or smaller pack sizes. However, **WPI** remains relatively expensive because it is more profitable for producers to divert whey toward higher-value derivatives rather than **WPC80**.

## Strategic Outlook
**Long-term Projections**
While new production capacity in America and Europe will increase supply, the structural imbalance remains; if **WPI** growth reaches its upper estimate of 11%, **WPC80** growth may be capped at around 4% due to limited raw material availability.

**Business Advice**
* Do not attempt to time the absolute bottom of the market for volume purchases; missing the window can lead to expensive replenishment during upward cycles.
* Maintain steady inventory levels as long as current pricing supports business profitability.
* If a business model cannot withstand high protein costs, consider structural changes such as product reformulation.

Action items: none returned.

takeaways.text: WPI went from around 7 euros a kilogram in 2023 to over 30 euros earlier this year; WPC80 held around 12 euros, then rocketed to 28 in about six weeks. WPC80 was the existential risk for brands because they had already moved their sourcing into it [00:16]. The slide puts WPI near EUR 32 a kilogram at the summer record and WPC80 up roughly sixfold since 2020, both "now correcting"; its chart (Vesper, EU monthly, December 2019 to October 2026) shows WPC80 at about EUR 5 in 2020 and 2023, peaking about EUR 12 in 2022 and about EUR 26 to 27 in mid 2026, and WPI at about EUR 8 in 2020, EUR 18 in 2022, EUR 7 in 2023 and about EUR 31 in mid 2026 (photo 2).

Demand drivers: traditional sports nutrition at 10% a year on Euromonitor, which he thinks is a big underestimate; GLP-1 users as incremental demand; protein going mainstream (Starbucks, Papa John's, Dunkin'); clear whey, which barely existed five years ago, is one of the fastest-selling parts of the category and is almost all whey [00:16]. The slide's figures: the 2024 global sports nutrition market splits 48% protein powders, 26% protein bars, 17% non-protein and 9% protein RTD, growing 8 to 10% a year; clear whey SKUs are up 35% year on year; 12% of US adults take a GLP-1 medication, with protein spend up 20% (KFF 2025, BCG 2026); Starbucks' protein drinks carry 15 to 36 g (photo 3).

Whey wins on taste and texture, not nutrition: "the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source." It is far easier to make a good-tasting product with whey than with most alternatives [00:16].

Supply: only 0.6% of liquid milk is whey protein (the rest by weight: water 87.3%, lactose 4.7%, fat 3.9%, casein 2.8%, minerals 0.7%); whey comes from cheese, and cheese production grows about 1.5% a year, so liquid whey does too, against demand growing over 10%. This is his most important conclusion [00:16] (photo 4) (photo 7).

The route from milk: cheese keeps the casein and fat; liquid whey goes through ultrafiltration and drying to WPC (35 to 80% protein), microfiltration or ion exchange to WPI (90% or more), then acidification or hydrolysis to clear or hydrolysed WPI; each step is a plant, and sweet whey powder (about 12% protein), permeate, lactose, demineralised whey (D70, D90, for infant nutrition) and whey cream are the other outlets for the same whey [00:16] (photo 4).

Factories are the first bottleneck ("phenomenally expensive" and slow to build; the slide: "CAPEX intensive, less flexible than people expect, takes years to start commercial production"); liquid whey is the second; byproducts are the third, "a major influencer of producer value", and WPI producers must also sell a fatty protein stream [00:16] (photo 6) (photo 7).

Over five years total whey protein supply grew just under 5% a year: global WPC80 plus WPI production rose 26%, from 414,494 t in 2020 to 521,800 t in 2025 (a 4.7% CAGR); WPI grew 15.0% a year (80,494 t to 161,800 t) at the expense of WPC80 at 1.5% (334,000 t to 360,000 t), which explains why WPC80 was undersupplied this year. Clear whey may be up to 25% of WPI (top of the estimate range; 40,450 t of the 161,800 t in 2025); ordinary instant WPI grew 8.6% a year, below the category [00:16] (photo 8) (photo 9).

New capacity: WPI expected to grow 7 to 11% a year, WPC80 4 to 7% (CAGR 2025 to 2030), but if WPI is at 11, WPC80 has to be more like 4 because there is not enough whey. Both are below underlying demand [00:16] (photo 11).

The capacity list: announced US additions (McCully Consulting, approximate) of 24,400 t of WPC80 and 7,500 t of WPI in 2026, 41,600 t and 20,300 t in 2027, 45,900 t and 22,900 t in 2028; in the UK, EU and Oceania, FrieslandCampina (WPI expansion), Fonterra (various speciality) and Polmlek (WPC and WPI) in 2026, Tirlan (WPC, WPI and clear) and Liprovit (WPI) in 2027, and Arla's mozzarella plant in 2028. He said the European list is not exhaustive, with some Eastern European producers he could not get information from [00:16] (photo 11).

Prices overshoot on behaviour, in both directions (the COVID example): buyers stock up when prices rise and sit out when they fall. The slide's cycle: longer lead times, inventory, demand rises, buyers compete for available material, prices rise, incentive to buy early, demand rises again, with the brand and consumer response feeding back into demand; the 2022 peak was logistics freeing up and buyers destocking, the 2023 trough buyers waiting as long as possible with stocks too low [00:16] (photo 13) (photo 15).

Now: WPC80 "has been falling pretty hard", WPI "still expensive, but definitely correcting"; new US factories set in motion three or four years ago are commissioning; producers have better uses for whey (WPI, WPC35, sweet whey powder), so WPC80 production should fall; MPC85 and other substitutes are rising and WPC80 and milk protein lines "should never meet" [00:16]. The weekly Vesper figures: between 25 August and 4 November 2026 WPC80 fell 40.7%, from EUR 27.00 to EUR 16.00 a kilogram, WPI fell 20.3%, from EUR 32.00 to EUR 25.50, and MPC85 rose 13.5%, from EUR 13.92 to EUR 15.80, meeting WPC80 at about EUR 16 on 4 November (photo 16) (photo 18).

The MPC85 line: brands substituted MPC85 (or MPI, caseins, plant proteins) into formulations, so those prices are rising while WPC80 falls; he quoted Keynes on markets staying irrational longer than you can stay solvent, so the lines touching does not mean they bounce apart at once, "but it can't go on forever" [00:16] (photo 18).

What decides the next move, from the slide: for WPC80 the bullish forces are strong other derivatives, rising alternatives and long-term protein demand, the bearish ones high inventories, powerful momentum and demand destruction; for WPI, bullish are its smaller share of brand costs, healthy inventories on both sides and being harder to replace, bearish are demand destruction and production increases due (photo 16).

Where prices go: "structurally rising but volatile"; the correction is under way and "may overshoot below trend... then demand pulls it back up". The schematic averages EU WPC80 and WPI (Vesper, monthly to October 2026) and the slide says the trend and forward path are "directional, not a forecast" [00:16] (photo 19).

Advice: do not try to be too clever with volume; buy steadily if the price works; whey will be and should be expensive; a business that cannot cope with this year's prices needs to change its model [00:16]. The three closing takeaways on the slide: "Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." (photo 20)
Nutrilution also sells niche, higher-value ingredients and advises buyers on whey and dairy protein sourcing, including cross-continental supply chains [00:16].

quotes.text: "Cheese is only growing one and a half percent a year, whereas waferaging demand is growing whatever figure we choose over over 10%." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]

"Certainly the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source. I think what people always care about is taste and texture. And whey protein is delicious." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
"If WPI is growing 11% a year, then WPC 80 has to be more like four because there's not enough whey." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
"So over the last few weeks, WPC80 has been falling pretty hard. WPI still expensive, but definitely correcting." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]

"Whey protein will be expensive. It should be expensive. It's the best protein source for so many uses. It's got a structural supply restriction, and the amount of protein is not really going away." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
"WPI is the growth engine. About a quarter of today's isolate is now Clear WPI, a category that barely existed in 2020." Slide (photo 9)
"Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." Slide (photo 20)

followups: Talk to Alan Johnstone (Nutrilution) about the WPI/WPC80 price series and the US and European capacity lists he showed; he invited conversations on sourcing strategy [00:16] (photo 11) (photo 18).

Cross-reference with Rousselot's WPC80 figure of 5.7k a tonne in 2023 to almost 32k in 2026 (whey-collagen-the-protein-power-couple); his Vesper series has WPC80 at about EUR 5 in 2023 and EUR 27.00 on 25 August 2026 (photo 2) (photo 16).
Check the Euromonitor 10% a year sports nutrition growth figure he cited; the slide says 8 to 10% year on year (photo 3) [00:16].
The slides credit Vesper (VPI, EU prices) for the price series and McCully Consulting for the US capacity data (photo 2) (photo 11).
