# Clicks to Community: Turning Digital Engagement into Brand Loyalty: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "SNS Panel - digital engagement", https://otter.ai/u/AFcS0eaniyWZMj-cu4IFkai0za0, recorded 9 Nov 2026 09:54, 40m 27s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:01] Speaker 1: Discover, evaluate, and purchase wellness products today. However, a recent report that we reported on at NI showed that there are more than 1,000 misleading food communication posts by influencers online with supplements the most frequent subject matter. So, while there's a huge opportunity to use social media to create communities, and really it's it's an essential part of brand strategy today, the industry is very much being watched carefully. And so with that, I'd like to just start the discussion with the brands that we have here on stage, because we have Shanae from Tonic and Julian from AG One, which are both huge online, massive online followings, but very different communication strategies. Both of your brands. So first of all, Sinead, would you give us a brief description of Tonic's online com strategy, and what is it about Tonic's content that makes people
[01:00] Speaker 2: stop scrolling? Yeah, sure. Thanks, Nikki. So, our kind of objective with our content is to make sure that everything that we do educates and just doesn't sell anything. So, we have flagship content which is called the Unsponsored Truth. So, Sunner, our founder of Tonic, goes around supermarkets and gives people in simple, realistic, healthy swaps that they can make in their everyday life to make themselves healthier. We've been running the content for about four years now, so we now have 1.9 million followers on social, and we get about 70 million views every single month, which, for a brand our size, is just insane and it's unheard of, and yeah, it's just incredible to have that kind of support from our community. I would say why our content works is because it's so simple, easy, and actionable. So you know, we kind of run the kind of brand now as a media business that happens to sell vitamins rather than actually what we are is we are a vitamin brand that essentially has overnight or not overnight the last four years I would say has just built this kind of following and you know vitamins came first and the kind of media is just what built the brand I would say you know why people engage with our content is probably because it's genuinely useful. It's 20 to 32nd clips. We post three times a day. We're educating you on just how to make one simple switch in your life to make yourself healthier. And I think from a kind of social perspective, people go to social for two things and two things only, and that is to be educated or to be entertained. And if you're not doing either of those two things as a brand, then you're gonna fail on social, frankly. And I think we've managed to just hit the nail on the head with kind of that education piece and give people simple, easy tricks that they can just take away into their everyday life. And I think why it works so well for us is because essentially we have a brand mission to expose the truth, expose the lies, build truth within the category to help people thrive. So every piece of content we do kind of sits within in that umbrella, and I think just genuinely be useful to people's lives is kind of why why you will like succeed?
[03:21] Speaker 1: Yeah. So key tip: don't try and sell your product.
[03:24] Speaker 2: Don't sell your product. Yeah. I mean, 99% of our content is not about our product, which a lot of people on our board and you know investors constantly question every day. And we stand by it because we bring people in a funnel, and as soon as they are ready to purchase a vitamin, they might ask us what the best vitamin is, or when they might get to the kind of supermarket shelf, they might look at the vitamin category and be like, "Oh, actually, I follow tonic. Let me just try theirs." But we're very, very soft and educational, and we yeah, I think 0.01% of our content is actually about our vitamins. Interesting. And so then
[04:00] Speaker 1: Julian, a key part of AG1's USP is the scientific backing, but science is notoriously difficult to try and communicate to someone in a social media post. So, how do you get around that? How much of your communication is about the research backing of the product?
[04:17] Speaker 3: So, we started by talking a lot about it, we talked a lot about our, you know, Goldstone, the clinical trials. We talked a lot about the the volume of third-party testing that we have in like all of our core markets, from the US to Europe to the UK to Australia, and people didn't care. And you know, Sinead has actually hit the nail on the head. Where people, particularly in a social environment, they come to be educated or entertained. But I would say with education that the key is to make it hyper relevant to that specific person to speak in their language, to understand what is the trigger point for them wanting to be interested in anything connected to to preventative health, which is something that's going to improve their lives, our mission has always been to empower people to take ownership of their health. So it's about figuring out what are the ways in which we can like give people the kind of the evidence they need to go after it. And what we've learned over time is, particularly a top of funnel, particularly in social. Too much evidence doesn't work. You know, we launch campaigns around in the US around WTF is NSF, NSF being the biggest kind of sports thing. We you know we did we did campaigns specifically about that on YouTube. We have a series called Dropping Hours, which is about trying to humanize this idea of all of the science that goes into our products, and that that has been quite successful. Again, because we're not selling anything, we're just providing information. But ultimately, social is about sparking curiosity, and it's about driving an association between a brand that has credibility to know what it's talking about without making the consumer necessarily do the work of like figuring out what does a gold standard clinical trial actually mean. You know, we need to make it relevant for them.
[06:11] Speaker 1: Okay, brilliant. And so, along the similar lines, then Dan, I'm interested to to know your point of view as a nutritionist. What would be your tips for how to simplify, perhaps simplify science or get across complicated messages or claims in a in a post?
[06:30] Speaker 4: Yeah, I think often when we think of the role of a nutritionist within a brand, it used to be very much like ambassador based, and you know certainly me being in the industry 10 years used to be very much kind of people wanting to offer commission or offer benefits for somebody to post the product and kind of just shout about how great it's. I think now with the emerging research and all of the different kind of I suppose angles that you can take on socials, whether that be like we said entertainment or kind of education. I think you know a nutritionist plays a big role in translating that information to the day-to-day consumer, working across professional sports myself, I find often that you know athletes don't really want the numbers, or you know you can shout as much as you want about the numbers. And as you were saying, you know certain things that you're doing in clinical trials, but what they want is the headline. But also to ensure that that's backed by the research. I think it's a really careful way of doing it because often I'll work with brands individually or as a as a business, and they'll want to put out some quite outlandish claims based on their their research. And sometimes you have to pull them back and say, you know, it's it's great that we can post about that on social media, but let's take the angle which ultimately the consumer is going to understand, and also that we're using the research to its best effect. I think there's a a lot of brands out there that maybe don't have that advisory from a nutritionist within industry that often will take a research paper or a cluster of research papers and want to use that directly with their brand and almost use the research to fit their mold, as opposed to using the research for what the intended purpose was. I think often a nutritionist not just navigates how to get it across to consumers, but can help them to navigate that research piece as well. Of how do we take genuine research and turn it into actionable insights and claims across social media?
[08:18] Speaker 1: Yeah, and you've touched on it a little bit there, perhaps, but I wanted to ask you what are some of the red flags, signs of when brands are not communicating science or health claims in the most transparent way?
[08:33] Speaker 4: How old we got? No, I think often you know a lot of the times it's it's the use of certain words that maybe don't present in the research because the words within the research are considered a little bit too dull or boring to present on social media. But the connotation of the words very different, and I think that's what really kind of trips me up when I'm looking at branding. Is they're using certain buzzwords that they know will get reaction because they potentially ran it through an AI model, for example, and it said this is the best kind of trending word that you can use. When actually the connotations can be very different, and I think often it comes out of like genuine accidental misleading, as opposed to like genuine trying to mislead a consumer. But I think it's it's the wording often that I think trips up a lot of brands is you know what you can and can't say around a product is a massive gray area, and it's not really you know regulated well. But I think you know as nutritionists, we can do a lot better job with brands to help them to communicate the message effectively.
[09:32] Speaker 1: Brilliant, thank you. And so Luca, to bring you in to talk about the regulations that are in play here, what are some of the key rules that marketers need to be aware of when they're marketing their products online.
[09:45] Luca Buccini (ESSNA): So thank you, Nikki. I think there are many rules now, and more are coming because, as you heard, marketing online is essential to communicate to consumers, to educate consumers. That's where our consumers, athletes, consumers go for information, go for education. So it's essential to be there, and regulators, regulators catching up. So we do have rules. We have rules about product communication, quite restrictive, nutrition and health claims regulation, which is very so that's the first piece of regulation in the UK. You have all the codes by the Advertising Authority. That that's really the most essential context in practice. And the other member states of the EU, the member states of the EU, have their own scenarios on influencer marketing and so on. So you have to check them as well. So that's very important. We have new pieces of regulations coming, and the Digital Finance Act. We don't know the text yet, but it's coming. So I think the overall effect of the current situation, which we have been communicating on social media, it has created tensions within teams, especially regulatory teams and marketing teams, all the time. And I think you know, if you are in our society, has has regulation held how how how the industry back? No, no, it's been a great way to communicate to communicate social media, increasing the AI as well. But I think there's been problems with the level playing field. Companies, especially responsible brands, have had to navigate that space. And eventually, what's happening is that regulators are starting to start to be concerned about discussions about new regulations coming up. So at this point, you have to look at the product specific regulations, rules about influence from marketing and social media, mainly by self-regulation bodies at this time, and and then upcoming regulations as well.
[11:53] Speaker 1: Okay, so what are some of the key missteps that you see brands making online?
[11:59] Luca Buccini (ESSNA): So the basic issues are related to disclosing advertising, but when you have content creators and and influencers, but but it should be the basics, but it still happens. But it's not disclosed, but it's an ad that it's paid for, or that there's been a gap behind it. That really happens all the time, and I've seen also some studies by self-regulation bodies, and it happens, still happens a lot that people don't disclose that. So, and then related that is that brands don't follow best practice in dealing with content creators and influencers and their own communication. So the responsibility is not allocated. There is been no training. That that's part of recurring issues. And then we have the as I mentioned the claims regulations and and differentiating as as you are saying when you are doing education, where you are communicating science, and when you are talking about the products, but and that's obviously a lot of issues. And I think the issues we are looking at more more closely are, I would say, two issues. The first is that it's not when a brand occasionally oversteps, but where there is a marketing strategy, it builds around non-compliance. So that that's a big issue. Sometimes you have to think not about only about specific messaging, but about your communication strategy, whether it's built around compliance or not. And sometimes brands have not been doing that, and they found out about regulations only when there's been a complaint and a regular action, and the second issue I think it's what also we are working with different regulators about this. When it's not just a brand, it's just like if the discourse about something is going off regulations, and so brands will see that the discussion is going in a certain direction, which is not compliant with signs, not compliant with regulations, and they would follow that type of information. That that's another area of concern. Would say so. I would say first check the basic in terms of federal content disclosure, and that type of requirements that you have. Then, if you differentiate education information from advertising of specific products, and then consider more broadly whether your strategy is compliant in itself.
[14:35] Speaker 2: Thank you. And so, I'm interested to know whether the brands on this panel, can share any times that they've perhaps misstepped or come a cropper with any previous posts on 81 or Tonic Health, either been picked up by the ASA or just or even just posts that haven't landed very well. Any examples that you'd be having to go? Yeah, I mean, our approach to social has always been like very like test and learn. So, the social team that's running the like this content to nearly our 2 million followers is one social media manager who's 22, and then a video editor who is a freelancer, basically, and that's all that is running our whole social channel, which is insane for a kind of audience that size. And we did run into an issue with the ESA where you know we shoot all of our kind of video content and we put it through a lens of have we made any claims? Have we ensured that we're saying the right thing? And we were talking about our new magnesium drink that had essentially just been launched. And we review every single piece of content with a lens of has it made any you know outlandish claims? Is it has it got you know like supports sleep or X Y Z? So we always make sure that the video content goes through that lens. However, the social cover that we have on our profile, which essentially doesn't go through any review system because it's just our 22-year-old social media manager who's creating these social covers. She wrote on the social cover the best sleep supplement in the market, and now we don't have that claim. We can't make that claim, and you know that essentially we put on our social we put on on the social covers, and it didn't go through any kind of review process. And the ASA pulled it up very rightly, and we immediately took it down. And you know it just essentially then put steps in place of how we actually do review every single element that goes into social because it is such a public channel. Now, since then, we kind of have a more I would say refined social process. So, with AI, hate to mention it, I know it's been mentioned already, but we have an AI system and an AI agent that essentially reviews every single piece of content to make sure that we are compliant and everything goes through the AI platform. And look, like we still get things wrong. We're posting 900 pieces of content across four channels every single month, and so naturally things do happen. Not necessarily with the ASA, but you know, will consumers or our followers will call us out if they've seen a different scientific paper that they think explains their perspective and view on things. You know, science is always moving. There's lots of opinions out there. There's lots of studies out there that kind of go against each other. So, if we believe that we've posted something that then might not necessarily be what our followers like, or they've sent us another study. We'll hold our hands up, like it's very easy on social media to just to delete a post and take it down. But we'll never do that. We always leave it live. We'll change the caption. We'll go back to all the comments. We sometimes jump on calls with our followers, leave them voice notes, explain where we were getting to with our version of the science, and we'll do response videos. And I think through doing all of that and being very honest and open and standing by our mistakes, how much I want to call them mistakes, but standing by you know our science and what we believe, I feel as though we're building trust because trust is really built in those small moments and owning your mistake, rather than just deleting yourself from the internet when you have done something that's not quite right.
[18:28] Speaker 5: Yeah, for sure.
[18:30] Speaker 3: I I mean I really I think that that idea of proactive transparency is so powerful. You know to to kind of build and develop your community within within a comment section, and what you guys are doing going beyond that with voice notes is amazing. And I think you're also bang on the money. Where I mean, Dan, you said it yourself. 99.9% of the time, these are marketing teams who simply don't have like who are doing the best that they can with the available information to them. There's no malice intended when stuff like this happens. I think perhaps the most amusing example of us having to go around the houses quite a lot on a TV script. So in the UK, Clearcast is like you're held to the absolute highest possible standard, and obviously making a TV TV, making a TV commercial costs a lot of money as well. So it was quite a high-stakes environment in which to be in. And about this time last year, we I was developing with my team the first ever European-wide TV commercial. And the premise of this TV commercial was the idea that there are two versions of you. There are there's the version pre AG1 or pre looking after yourself, pre workout, pre whatever that doesn't kind of have that amazing morning routine. And then there's the version of you that does. They're a little bit more sprightly. They've got a bit more energy. They kind of they know what they're doing. And we we created that TVC by hiring two sets of identical twins, and they literally played off each other, so one of them was was kind of where they do one, and one what there wasn't. And the opening line of the TV commercial that we worked with for about three months of pre-production development was, "Ever wonder what the best version of you looks like?" Clear cast, no thanks. So we then went around with him, we were like, "What about a better version of you?" Not allowed that. What about a slightly better version of you? Still can get it over the line. And in the end, we landed on a line that was approved by them. Same version of you. Which was another version of you. Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help? And in the end, because these people were supporting this this this version, this AG1 drinker in the creative was actually helping out the person who was feeling a little bit more tired, a little bit less kind of energetic in the morning. That line actually worked a lot better because they were literally a helping hand in the TVC, and I think what we what we what we practice, or at least what we try to practice internally all the time, is this idea that creative constraint is a very powerful way to deliver better communication, and we talk a lot about restraint being its own version of power in our space, where so many businesses oversell and underdeliver, and we we actively pursue the opposite dynamic. We let that science, that kind of mid funnel work, we call it, which is the sort of the education piece, when people are in that consideration set, we let people come to us, read the information, understand the science for themselves. We stand at the top, really being very deliberate about trying not to do that, and kind of so far it's working. The complication is always, and Nikki, you and I have talked about this before, is when you work with partners or creators who experience and feel amazing things from a product. I'm so proud to work for a brand that has a product like AG1. Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Industry experts discussed effective digital engagement strategies, regulatory compliance, and the role of science in social media marketing for wellness brands.

## Content Strategy
**Sinead** from **Tonic** explained that their strategy focuses on education rather than direct selling, utilizing a "media business" model to build community. By providing simple, actionable health swaps through flagship content like **Unsponsored Truth**, they have reached 1.9 million followers and 70 million monthly views. **Julian** from **AG1** noted that while scientific evidence is a USP, too much technical detail fails on social media; instead, they focus on humanizing science through series like **Dropping Hours** to spark curiosity.

**Dan**, a nutritionist, highlighted the importance of translating complex research into "headlines" that consumers can understand. He warned against using buzzwords or AI-generated language that may have different connotations than the original research, potentially leading to accidental misinformation.

## Regulatory Compliance
**Luca** from **ESSNA** outlined the complexities of navigating UK **Advertising Authority** codes and varying EU member state regulations regarding influencer marketing. He identified several key risks:
* Failure to disclose paid advertisements or partnerships.
* Marketing strategies built around non-compliance rather than adherence to rules.
* Brands following non-compliant discourse trends seen in comment sections.

**Sinead** shared a specific misstep where a social media manager used an unreviewed claim ("best sleep supplement") on a profile cover, resulting in an **ASA** intervention. To prevent this, **Tonic** now uses an **AI** agent to review content for compliance. **Julian** also discussed the difficulty of working with creative agencies like **Clearcast**, noting how strict regulations forced a shift from "best version of you" to more compliant messaging in TV commercials.

## Future Trends
The panel addressed the impact of **AI** on the industry:
* **Julian** argued that while **AI** helps scale content, human insight must remain at both the beginning and end of the creative process to ensure quality and empathy.
* **Luca** suggested that regulators will likely introduce new rules as **AI** agents begin to provide personalized nutritional advice and visual information.
* **Dan** observed that athletes remain highly impressionable, often seeking a competitive edge through unverified claims found on platforms like **TikTok Shop**.

How will upcoming regulations like the **Digital Finance Act** specifically impact the intersection of **AI** and nutrition marketing?

Action items (as returned):
- Speaker 2 - : Ensure AI-assisted content begins with a human consumer insight and ends with human review and rewriting, using AI only to help scale or refine content in the middle of the process.
- Speaker 2 - : Maintain a human-in-the-loop content process: start each AI-assisted message with a human insight, use AI only for intermediate scaling or refinement, and finish with human review and rewriting.

# Fuelling the female runner: from paper to podium to partnerships: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "James Morton - SNS", https://otter.ai/u/4ZvcEK7EZ-gYpMKB02e7T9ELdgw, recorded 9 Nov 2026 11:16, 26m 59s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: And in the absence of ingesting carbohydrate during exercise, then that carbohydrate oxidation that we're measuring is a reflection of the carbohydrate that's stored in liver and muscle. And so, when we're measuring carbohydrate in grams per minute in terms of its use, actually, what we're measuring really is the breakdown of both liver glycogen and muscle glycogen rebels, and unfortunately, our body only stores a little bit of the amount, and unfortunately, that could run out within two hours of exercise, depending on the intensity and so on. So, I want to show you some muscle glycogen data. If you haven't seen it before, this is a picture of a muscle biopsy. We've probably taken over 1000 muscle biopsies in Liverpool in the last 10 years, and one of the papers that we did back in 2021 was this paper that was published in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise, and this was a study where we took both male and female rec racingly active runners. We took biopsies from both the vastus lateralis muscle and also the gastrocnemius muscle before and after three different types of training sessions. So this was part of salmon beef postoptral studies, and here you can see the differences in the cohorts, both males and females. As you would expect, the females were lighter, and they had a lower absolute VO2 max, their lactate threshold, and their lactate turn point, which is a marker of Roman fitness, occurred at a much slower running speed. But it's very typical of recreationally active runners, and by no means elite runners. Just your standard club runner and the average recreational runner. Now, what we did in that study was we brought them into the lab on the evening of day one, and we asked them to perform a bout of standardized exercise, we then fed them carbohydrate before they went to sleep that evening. We then fed them carbohydrate throughout day two, so we actually gave them foods that was all prepackaged and customized to their body mass. On day three, they also had six grams per kilogram of carbohydrate, and then they came in the afternoon at 3 p.m. and we then asked them to do three different types of training sessions in a repeated measures randomized design. And we took muscle biopsies from both the vastus lateralis and the gastric nemaeus muscle. And in the interest of time, I'm just going to show you the gastric nemesis data. So again, here's an illustration of a muscle biopsy from the gastric music. I must prefer getting these biopsies done myself because you lie in your front, you don't really know when the needle's going in compared to the thigh. But it's not as painful as what it looks. Here you can see a photograph of one of the female participants running around the track in Liverpool just after she had that biopsy. What I'm going to show you is data from three different types of training sessions. So the first session, we actually took these runners on a 10-mile road run around Liverpool. So we rode on a bike beside them while they were running. We were controlling what speed they were running at. We asked them to run at a speed corresponding to their lactate threshold. So you can see that the males were running at about 12.5 kilometers per hour. The females just over 10 kilometers per hour. Of course, the men took less time to run that 10 miles, 77 minutes versus 96 minutes in the female participants. And what you see here is the muscle glycogen data. So each white dot represents an individual participant, and the first thing to note was that the men seemed to store more glycogen than what the females did before they ran this 10-mile road run. We took biopsies after the 10 miles, and both sexes then finished pretty much with glycogen depletion, so no differences between groups. Second session that we did was we took them to the running track in Liverpool and we asked them to perform eight times 800 meter efforts, pretty much at a running speed corresponding to their VO two max. So the men were running just over 16 kilometers, the females close to 14 kilometers. That corresponded to a session duration of 23 minutes versus 28 minutes, and again we seen that the female participants had less resting muscle glycogen than the male participants, but they finished with similar glycogen status after performing that training session. And the last session we did was three times 10 minute efforts, also on the running track, that corresponded to the speed of lactate turnpoint, so almost like a tempo type session. Once again, the female participants presented with less absolute glycogen than the men before the session would finish with similar absolute glycogen stores. Now, people have interpreted this that females then store less glycogen than men, and therefore we need some sort of specific sport nutritional guidance. Well, there is a nuance to that study, and if you remember the body mass differences, and remember how we're prescribing carbohydrate intake, we're prescribing it in grams per kilogram body mass. So, because the women were lighter than the men, in absolute terms, they're ingesting a lower absolute quantity of carbohydrate, and actually, when you go through some of the limited studies in the literature, what you quickly see that is, if you give a man and a woman the same absolute amount of carbohydrate, which means that the females might then have to ingest eight or nine grams per kilogram body mass versus six grams per kilogram water mass, there isn't really any differences in glycogen storage. So actually, our interpretation of the literature is: for a given relative intake, then female participants may present with slightly less absolute glycogen. But if you ensure that they consume the same absolute amount of carbohydrate, then you don't really see any differences in glycogen storage. What I should also say is that these differences in glycogen concentration, when you express them in grams within the muscle itself, we're talking very very small differences here, less than five grams differences within the gastrocnemius muscle, as an example, and such small differences don't really translate to any practical differences in terms of the nutritional guidelines. So, at least in terms of glycogen storage, there's probably real trivial differences in storage, which don't manifest to any differences in practical sport nutrition guidelines, especially if you're a recreationally active runner and you're not really competing at that top end. Now, the second part of this morning session, I then want to switch our attention to what happens when we ingest carbohydrate during exercise. And so, you've already seen this slide. When you measure carbohydrate metabolism and we report it in grams per minute, it's a reflection of both liver glycogen and muscle glycogen. I've already showed you some muscle glycogen depletion, but when we're actually ingesting carbohydrate during exercise, we digest it, we absorb it. It enters the bloodstream and it goes to the liver, and the liver then decides whether to actually hold that carbohydrate or also put it back into the circulation to go to muscle. And what actually happens is that when you consume carbohydrate during exercise, you actually break down less of your existing stores, so you lose less liver glycogen, you use less muscle glycogen, so that you're protecting your limited stores, and you have more for later on during exercise. And so now, when we're measuring carbohydrate use, let's say it's three grams a minute. That three grams a minute is a reflection of liver use, muscle use, but also what you're ingesting during exercise. Now, unfortunately, much of our understanding of carbohydrate ingestion during exercise has been done on cyclists. There's very very limited information on runners, so we partnered with England Athletics just a couple of years ago, and we were very fortunate to get some real high quality runners into the lab. And we did this with a cohort of male runners and also female participants. The male data we actually published last year in the Journal of Applied Physiology, it received quite a lot of attention at the time. So that data is published. The female data that I'm about to show you isn't yet published. It's in its second stage of peer review. Hopefully, it will be accepted in the coming weeks. Here's here's the the baseline characteristics of the men and the women in this study: very, very high fitness. So you can see their personal best in the marathon for the men was around two hours 20. Personal best of the females was about two hours 40. Their running speeds at lactate threshold 15 kilometers and almost 14 kilometers. At lactate turn point 16 kilometers, 15 kilometers. I'm sure a lot of people in the audience actually do run themselves, and you're probably thinking, could I run at that speed? I'm not sure. This is like. I wanted to show you the experimental design that we did in this story. So we always control what people eat before they come to the lab because we're trying to get real tight these high nutritional status. So we fed them both a high carbohydrate diet on day one, eight grams per kilogram body mass. They came back on the morning of day two. We fed them breakfast in the lab, two grams per kilogram carbohydrate body mass. We then asked them to run for two hours, and the first 15 minutes, two hours, 15 minute period just below lactate threshold, and we then did 90 minutes just below lactate turnpoint, which was simulated race pace. So this is pretty much the pace that these participants were running their marathon at, and so actually this was like the highest caliber of participants ever studied in the lab, you can see that by the running speeds, and more importantly, it was the first time that anyone that actually fed either 60 grams, 90 grams, or 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour. 60 and 90 is like the traditional sport nutrition guideline recommendations, with 90 being the upper limit. 120 is the emerging recommendation that was definitely seeing a lot of cyclists consume, but this had never really been studied in the rumors before. I'll just take you through the data and I'll explain the data. So on the left-hand side, this is what we call whole-body carbohydrate oxidation, and you will have heard me speak about this many times already, and we measure that in grams per minute. So effectively, what you see at the start of exercise is the men are burning up around 2.5 to 3 grams of carbohydrates per minute. There comes a point during exercise when your rate of whole-body carbohydrate use starts to decline, and the reason why it's starting to decline is, of course, because you're running out of liver glycogen, you're running out of muscle glycogen, and your body then shifts its reliance towards burning fat as a fuel. And that's the whole rationale for consuming carbohydrate during that time. We're trying to maintain our whole body rates of use as long as we can, because carbohydrate is a very economic fuel when compared to using fat as a fuel, but even when you consume those traditional sport nutrition guidelines of 60 grams an hour, after about 60 minutes, we still see a decline in whole body use. With 90 grams, we also see a decline, but with 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour were better able to maintain our whole body rates during exercise. Here you can see the female data on the right. If you look very closely, the biggest thing that you'll see differences between the sexes is that females burn on average around half a gram to one gram per minute less, and that's probably because they're smaller to start with. So yes, they're running at a lower absolute speed, but they're smaller, so it requires less of an absolute carbohydrate cost. But again, you can see that decline in whole-body carbohydrate oxidation during exercise, even when consuming 60 and 90 grams per hour was 10 years ago was the sport nutrition recommended advice. Now, what I'll now show you is the contribution of carbohydrate and fat to energy expenditure. So, carbohydrate is in the green, and fat or lipid is in the red. And what happens during exercise is we get this crossover effect. In cycling, this happens in about two hours. In runners, it happens much faster. And so, with 60 grams of carbohydrate per hour, we see a crossover effect after about 60 minutes of exercise. Lots of people will tell me that athletes are carbohydrate dependent, and that when you're running fast, you're carbohydrate dependent. In the second bar of exercise, these athletes are not carbohydrate dependent at all. They're fat dependent. The majority of their energy is being provided by fat, despite the fact that they've had a high carbohydrate diet the day before, a high carbohydrate breakfast, and they've also consumed 60 grams per hour. They are still effectively running out of carbohydrate because they're now burning more fat as a fuel. So we get this crossover effect in both men and women with 60 grams an hour. If we take 90 grams an hour, we don't prevent the crossover. We just basically shift it to the right. So you're maintaining carbohydrate dependency for longer, which is a good thing because it's more of an economic fuel. It costs less oxygen to burn carbohydrate than what it does fat. And actually, when we consume 120 grams of carbohydrate per hour, not only have you shifted the crossover point, you've completely prevented it. And so now you see pathways actually are being carbohydrate dependent for the whole duration of the two hours, and so clearly shifting that dose by 30 gram per hour increments. I see it on social media that it doesn't do anything. It has profound impacts on metabolism. It completely changes how you metabolize fuel, and now you're becoming carbohydrate dependent. I like the previous cycling study that I showed at the very beginning. What we also did with the carbohydrate was enrich it with carbon-13 stable isotopes, and so what that means is that when we ingest that carbohydrate, we can then measure the rate of appearance of carbon-13 on the expired breath, and then we can then quantify exactly how much is the carbohydrate that's being tested? Exactly going for fuel during exercise. Men on the left, women on the right. Each stock represents an individual participant. So you can see with 60 grams an hour, both sentences are burning around one gram a minute. With 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour, we're now getting close to 1.3, 1.4 grams a minute, and with 120 grams per hour, and this is some of the highest rates of oxidation ever reported in literature. We do see individual males and females who are capable of oxidizing between 80 and 100 percent of what they're ingesting. So this was the first time it had ever been reported in the literature, and so at least in that study, it's pretty clear to me that men and women don't differ in their ability to digest and oxidize carbohydrate during exercise, even these high amounts and running at these high speeds. And what does this mean from a performance perspective, well, we didn't actually measure performance in that study. We were more interested in the metabolism, but we did measure running economy. And so, this is the amount of oxygen that it costs to run at a given speed. And actually, what you can see is, with 120 grams per hour in both sexes, it reduces the amount of oxygen that it takes you to run at the same absolute speed, and we call that running economy. And so, for those of you in the room who are runners, you'll probably be very familiar with Nike's claim when they first launched the Vaporfly that their shoes improved running economy by 4%. While carbohydrate does exactly the same, we get an improvement in running economy between two and 3%, depending on sexes, and so I'm I'm pretty sure that that's why you are seeing a lot of these running records and performances improve. Not only are they wearing better shoes, but they're also fueling like they've never fuelled before. So the take-home message from part two of this morning's presentation would be as follows, and I should say that we did see some more gastrointestinal symptoms in the females than we did in the males, which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length and so on. But there's definitely not a difference in their ability to digest and oxidize that carbohydrate. Maybe slight differences in their ability to tolerate that carbohydrate, especially when running at those streets. I finally, as I've come so close, so how should both men and women fuel their run in 2026? So we just wrote a paper a few months ago in the Journal of Nutrition where we tried to summarize a lot of this literature, and we also tried to put together a little fueling matrix to help people make informed decisions, and so rather than just saying that you need between 30 and 90 grams of carbohydrates depending on duration, actually we have to also consider both intensity and duration. So on the left-hand slide, I have a lot of exercise intensity according to different languages. They do often do percentage of the U.S. zone one, zone two, zone three, all the way up to zone five, or around the last year, whether it's the moderate, the heavier, the severe domain. But the point being is that when you exercise at higher intensities, that requires a higher cost of carbohydrate use. So your whole body rate of carbohydrate use may range from one gram a minute to five grams a minute, depending on how fast you exercise, how hard you turn the pedals, and so on. Now, if you want to maintain that rate of carbohydrate use during exercise, and as you see in the marketing studies, it's probably a good thing to do so because it will improve your economy. If you want to maintain your rate of use, then you have to ingest carbohydrates during exercise. But it all depends on what you're trying to do. So if you're to go out tonight, maybe you'll go home tomorrow when you leave the conference. You might go for a little 60-minute run at very low intensity. You probably don't need any carbohydrate. If you're deciding to shift through the zones and you're then going again 60 minutes but at a higher intensity, then it's probably between 30 and 60 grams an hour. If you're to go for a longer duration, so now we're getting into team sports type activity or the half marathon type distance, then again you may want to push up towards 90 grams. If you're then going between two and three lives, there's a definite rationale to go towards 120 grams. I would say, actually, and again, this isn't me being Iron at all, but I think I really understand that element of this slide because we've lived it for 20 years. What I don't think the industry really understands is what happens when you go out to 34567, and eight hours in the ultra endurance world, and that will be a big feature of our science strategy over the next few years to try and really articulate metabolism and provide solutions for that exercise duration scenario. How do you bring all this to life? Well, just like men, women may also not know the numbers to recommend the guidelines, and they also need to practice their fueling. And for those of you who were at this conference last year, you may recognize some of this data. But this was a paper that we published with Nike, or it's in the movie. And we asked email runners about their barriers to fueling. It became pretty clear that they probably don't understand the numbers, but they might have some cancer intestine symptoms that they need to treat. Men also have these symptoms, so it's not unique to females. And so this time last year, I actually stood in a room with the executives of Nike from their running team, and we were presenting a lot of that data in London actually a year ago, and we decided to then partner together to try and educate three-year runners on their fueling requirements. So this year we had a global partnership with Nike around their After Doctor. The After Doctor is of course all around promoting safe environments to women for women to run in. It's across seven cities across the world, and actually we partnered with Nike not really on a product creation, but all actually about education. And so we came up with a whole education package to educate these runners from training all the way through to race day. Yes, we did co-brand products, and the products were co-branded around the different durations because that event has 10 k races as well as half marathon races. But we tried to take those female runs through a targeted education pathway to really make the numbers simple and help them understand different products for different durations, different intensities, and so on. And that was a really successful partnership. I should say we'll be working very closely with Nike over the coming years, so we want that space. Well, if I was to leave you with a take-home message this morning, and hopefully you'll agree with the data that I presented today, hopefully you'll agree with the following statement. I would say that the biggest buyer to fueling the female runner is not biological. They don't have special guts or special muscles that we need to consider. Actually, I would say the biggest buyer, like men actually as well, is educational, and so therefore, but females in particular come from a world where under fueling has probably been at play. A big culture of under fueling, certainly my experience of both team sports and endurance sports. And I do think the industry is becoming slightly confused and all too aware of of many messages that we see that you're on day 15 of your cycle. Take this versus day 20, I don't believe in it at all. I must admit. So for me, fueling is less about tailoring to your hormones. It's less about fueling to your menstrual cycle. Actually, it's just about fueling for the work required. If you're working with a female athlete, the way that I do it is to treat them as an athlete first, and their sex might come into the conversation as we go down that coaching pathway. summary.Summary: James Morton (Science in Sport) argued that the biggest barrier to fuelling the female runner is educational, not biological [00:00] (photo 20). From a 2021 Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise study of recreational runners with muscle biopsies before and after three sessions, women started with less muscle glycogen than men but finished the same; the gap was under 5 g in the gastrocnemius and disappears when the same absolute carbohydrate is given, so it does not change practical guidance [00:00]. In an England Athletics study of elite runners (marathon bests about 2:20 for men and 2:40 for women) fed 60, 90 or 120 g of carbohydrate an hour over a two-hour run (15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold, 90 minutes at 94% of lactate turnpoint, 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold), 120 g prevented the crossover from carbohydrate to fat in both sexes, exogenous oxidation reached about 1 g a minute at 60 g, 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g and some individuals oxidised 80 to 100 percent of what they took at 120 g, and running economy improved by two to 3% in both sexes; the male data is Ravikanti et al. (2025) in the Journal of Applied Physiology and the female data is under revision [00:00] (photo 2) (photo 6) (photo 7). He showed a fuelling framework from Morton et al. (2026) in the Journal of Nutrition that sets carbohydrate by intensity and duration, from none for an easy hour to 120 g an hour dual source for a marathon, and described the SiS partnership with Nike's After Dark Tour as an education programme in seven cities with a co-branded race pack and a range "designed for her" [00:00] (photo 12) (photo 17) (photo 19). He does not believe in fuelling to the menstrual cycle: treat the female athlete as an athlete first [00:00] (photo 20). In the Q&A he said power analysis supports nine participants, fat-free mass may be the better dosing basis for women, and dual-source blends are needed at 90 and 120 g but not below 90 minutes [22:54], [23:48], [24:34], [25:17].
summary.Key takeaways:
- In the 2021 study (recreational runners, 6 g per kg carbohydrate on the day, a 10-mile run at lactate threshold, 8 x 800 m, 3 x 10 minutes), women began with less muscle glycogen than men but both finished similarly depleted; the difference was less than 5 g in the gastrocnemius and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].
- The gap is a dosing artefact: carbohydrate is prescribed per kilogram, so lighter women take less in absolute terms; given the same absolute amount, "there isn't really any differences in glycogen storage". His hedge: for a given relative intake women "may present with slightly less absolute glycogen" [00:00].
- Study design: 8 g per kg carbohydrate on day one, a 2 g per kg breakfast on day two, then 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold, 90 minutes at 94% of lactate turnpoint (simulated race pace) and 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold; the 60 g an hour condition was maltodextrin only, the 90 and 120 g conditions 1:1 maltodextrin and fructose [00:00] (photo 2).
- Elite runners (men about 2:20, women about 2:40 marathon bests) ran two hours after 8 g per kg the day before and 2 g per kg at breakfast; 60 g an hour gave a crossover to fat after about 60 minutes, 90 g shifted it right, 120 g prevented it for the full two hours [00:00]. The slides show the crossover at about 60 to 75 minutes on 60 g in both sexes and no crossover on 120 g in either, with men's carbohydrate oxidation on 120 g holding at about 3.0 to 3.2 g a minute from 45 to 105 minutes (photo 3) (photo 4) (photo 6).
- Exogenous oxidation (carbon-13): about 1 g a minute at 60 g an hour, close to 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g, and at 120 g some men and women oxidised between 80 and 100 percent of intake, "some of the highest rates of oxidation ever reported"; men and women do not differ in ability to digest and oxidise carbohydrate [00:00]. The slide's peak means, read from the chart: men about 1.0, 1.5 and 1.8 g a minute at 60, 90 and 120 g; women about 1.0, 1.45 and 1.75; seven to eight participants a group; "120 > 90 > 60 g" in both sexes (photo 7).
- Running economy improved by between two and 3% at 120 g an hour, against Nike's 4% Vaporfly claim; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00]. The conclusion slide: 120 g an hour "reduces the oxygen cost of running (i.e. improves running economy) compared with traditional CHO guidelines of 60-90 g/h" (photo 9).
- Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms than men, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; tolerance may differ slightly, oxidation does not [00:00]. The slide's wording: "individual variations in rates of exogenous CHO oxidation and gastrointestinal symptoms warrant CHO personalisation strategies" (photo 9).
- Fuelling matrix (Journal of Nutrition): an easy 60-minute run needs no carbohydrate; 60 minutes at higher intensity 30 to 60 g an hour; team sport or half marathon towards 90 g; two to three hours a definite rationale for 120 g. Ultra-endurance (three to eight hours) is the gap SiS's science strategy will work on [00:00].
- The framework in full (Morton et al. 2026, Journal of Nutrition) plots intensity (zones 1 to 5; moderate under 2 mmol/L, heavy 2 to 4, severe over 4) against duration: under an hour, 0 g, 0 to 30 g or 30 to 60 g single source for HIT (mouth rinse, drinks, gels); one to two hours, 30 to 60 g single source, 60 to 90 g single or dual source for soccer, 90 g dual source for a half marathon (drinks, gels, chews); two to three hours, 60 to 90 g single or dual, 90 to 120 g dual, 120 g dual source for a marathon (drinks, gels, chews, bars); beyond three hours cycling stages, beyond six ultra (photo 12).
- The barriers: female marathoners "do not know the numbers" (psychological capability; participant 18 took her first gel at 7 or 8 miles and went by what others do) and tolerating carbohydrate during a race can be a barrier (physical capability; participant 13 aimed for about 80 g an hour, felt her stomach "was not happy" in the heat and skipped her last two gels); like men, female runners need to practise fuelling in training (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15).
- SiS partnered with Nike After Dark (women's night races in seven cities) on education rather than product creation, with co-branded products by race duration; the partnership continues [00:00]. The Sydney 21K race pack sells at $40.00 ("Fuel your night"): eight packs of Run Fuel Endurance energy gels (3 x 60 ml), Run Hydro+ electrolyte powder (4.3 g), a Run Fuel Endurance energy chew (50 g) and Run Recovery Endurance powder (73 g) (photo 17).
- The Nike x SiS After Dark range, "designed for her", laid out for 10K and half marathon: Run Fuel Isotonic gel (22 g single-source carbohydrate; before and during), Run Fuel Endurance gel (40 g dual source; during), Run Fuel Endurance chew (40 g dual source, 1:0.8 glucose to fructose; before and during), Run Hydro+ sugar-free electrolytes (350 mg sodium; before, during and after), Run Recovery (25 g single-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) and Run Recovery Endurance (40 g dual-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) (photo 19).
- "The biggest barrier to fueling the female runner is not biological... it is educational"; under-fuelling is cultural; he does not believe in day-of-cycle fuelling messages [00:00]. The closing slide: the barrier "is not likely a biological limitation i.e. their gut or their muscles" but "lack of knowledge and awareness of the guidelines", in "a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent"; fuelling "is less about hormones and tailoring to the menstrual cycle, put simply, it is about fuelling for the work required" (photo 20).
- Q&A: nine participants gives 80% power because a 30 g step changes oxidation by 0.3 to 0.4 g a minute [22:54]; women should probably be dosed per kilogram of fat-free mass, but it is hard to measure [23:48]; 60 g was maltodextrin only, 90 and 120 g dual source; dual source is needed above about 90 minutes and lowers oxidation at 60 g [24:34], [25:17].
summary.For Vita Actives: Nothing in the talk touches our ingredients: no protein, creatine or pre-workout was mentioned from the stage, and the only protein on a slide is the 25 g (including 5 g collagen) in the two Run Recovery drinks of the Nike x SiS range, source not stated (photo 19). The value is customer insight: SiS builds its pitch on its own trials (England Athletics, Nike), published papers and a one-slide framework, and its chief science voice is openly sceptical of claims he sees on social media [00:00] (photo 12). My reading is that a sports nutrition brand of this kind expects a supplier to bring trial data and a one-slide rule of thumb, not a benefit list, and that is the standard CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea material should meet. The gut tolerance point (more GI symptoms in women at high intakes, and a runner skipping gels on an unhappy stomach) is adjacent to the digestibility story for a clear pea protein (photo 15) (my reading). The clear recovery drinks carry 25 g protein in a clear format for women runners, which is the format IsoClr: Pea is made for (my reading). Relevance low: carbohydrate fuelling, outside our range.

files.name: otter-summary.md
files.text:
Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

James Morton presented research on carbohydrate metabolism, glycogen storage, and fueling strategies for runners.

## Glycogen Research
**James** discussed a 2021 study involving male and female recreational runners to examine muscle glycogen depletion in the *vastus lateralis* and *gastrocnemius* muscles.
* **Key Findings**: While females showed lower absolute resting glycogen stores, this was attributed to lower body mass and carbohydrate intake prescribed in grams per kilogram. When consuming the same absolute amount of carbohydrate, no significant differences in storage were observed.
* **Practical Implications**: The differences in glycogen concentration are trivial (less than five grams) and do not necessitate different nutritional guidelines for recreational runners.

## Fueling Strategies
**James** shared new, unpublished data regarding high-performance runners (marathon personal bests of 2:20 for men and 2:40 for women) to evaluate carbohydrate oxidation rates.
* **Oxidation Rates**: Consuming 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour prevented the "crossover effect" where the body shifts from carbohydrate to fat metabolism, maintaining carbohydrate dependency for the full two hours.
* **Running Economy**: Ingesting 120 grams per hour improved running economy by 2% to 3%, comparable to the impact of advanced footwear technology.
* **Fueling Matrix**: **James** proposed a strategy based on intensity and duration:
    1. Low intensity (<60 mins): No carbohydrate required.
    2. Moderate intensity (60 mins): 30–60 grams per hour.
    3. Long duration (Half marathon): Up to 90 grams per hour.
    4. Ultra-endurance (2–3+ hours): Target 120 grams per hour using dual-source blends (maltodextrin and fructose).

## Technical Discussion
During the Q&A, **Olivia** queried the methodology and specific nutrient types used in the studies.
* **Sample Size**: **James** confirmed that power analysis supported the sample size of nine participants due to the strong physiological effect observed when increasing doses by 30 grams per hour.
* **Nutrient Composition**: The 60g/hour dose utilized maltodextrin only, while 90g and 120g doses used dual-source maltodextrin and fructose to ensure gastrointestinal tolerance and maximize oxidation.
* **Open Questions**: Would prescribing carbohydrate in grams per kilogram of fat-free mass provide a more accurate dose for female athletes?

Action items: none returned.

takeaways.text: In the 2021 study (recreational runners, 6 g per kg carbohydrate on the day, a 10-mile run at lactate threshold, 8 x 800 m, 3 x 10 minutes), women began with less muscle glycogen than men but both finished similarly depleted; the difference was less than 5 g in the gastrocnemius and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].

The gap is a dosing artefact: carbohydrate is prescribed per kilogram, so lighter women take less in absolute terms; given the same absolute amount, "there isn't really any differences in glycogen storage". His hedge: for a given relative intake women "may present with slightly less absolute glycogen" [00:00].

Study design: 8 g per kg carbohydrate on day one, a 2 g per kg breakfast on day two, then 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold, 90 minutes at 94% of lactate turnpoint (simulated race pace) and 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold; the 60 g an hour condition was maltodextrin only, the 90 and 120 g conditions 1:1 maltodextrin and fructose [00:00] (photo 2).

Elite runners (men about 2:20, women about 2:40 marathon bests) ran two hours after 8 g per kg the day before and 2 g per kg at breakfast; 60 g an hour gave a crossover to fat after about 60 minutes, 90 g shifted it right, 120 g prevented it for the full two hours [00:00]. The slides show the crossover at about 60 to 75 minutes on 60 g in both sexes and no crossover on 120 g in either, with men's carbohydrate oxidation on 120 g holding at about 3.0 to 3.2 g a minute from 45 to 105 minutes (photo 3) (photo 4) (photo 6).

Exogenous oxidation (carbon-13): about 1 g a minute at 60 g an hour, close to 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g, and at 120 g some men and women oxidised between 80 and 100 percent of intake, "some of the highest rates of oxidation ever reported"; men and women do not differ in ability to digest and oxidise carbohydrate [00:00]. The slide's peak means, read from the chart: men about 1.0, 1.5 and 1.8 g a minute at 60, 90 and 120 g; women about 1.0, 1.45 and 1.75; seven to eight participants a group; "120 > 90 > 60 g" in both sexes (photo 7).

Running economy improved by between two and 3% at 120 g an hour, against Nike's 4% Vaporfly claim; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00]. The conclusion slide: 120 g an hour "reduces the oxygen cost of running (i.e. improves running economy) compared with traditional CHO guidelines of 60-90 g/h" (photo 9).

Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms than men, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; tolerance may differ slightly, oxidation does not [00:00]. The slide's wording: "individual variations in rates of exogenous CHO oxidation and gastrointestinal symptoms warrant CHO personalisation strategies" (photo 9).

Fuelling matrix (Journal of Nutrition): an easy 60-minute run needs no carbohydrate; 60 minutes at higher intensity 30 to 60 g an hour; team sport or half marathon towards 90 g; two to three hours a definite rationale for 120 g. Ultra-endurance (three to eight hours) is the gap SiS's science strategy will work on [00:00].

The framework in full (Morton et al. 2026, Journal of Nutrition) plots intensity (zones 1 to 5; moderate under 2 mmol/L, heavy 2 to 4, severe over 4) against duration: under an hour, 0 g, 0 to 30 g or 30 to 60 g single source for HIT (mouth rinse, drinks, gels); one to two hours, 30 to 60 g single source, 60 to 90 g single or dual source for soccer, 90 g dual source for a half marathon (drinks, gels, chews); two to three hours, 60 to 90 g single or dual, 90 to 120 g dual, 120 g dual source for a marathon (drinks, gels, chews, bars); beyond three hours cycling stages, beyond six ultra (photo 12).

The barriers: female marathoners "do not know the numbers" (psychological capability; participant 18 took her first gel at 7 or 8 miles and went by what others do) and tolerating carbohydrate during a race can be a barrier (physical capability; participant 13 aimed for about 80 g an hour, felt her stomach "was not happy" in the heat and skipped her last two gels); like men, female runners need to practise fuelling in training (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15).

SiS partnered with Nike After Dark (women's night races in seven cities) on education rather than product creation, with co-branded products by race duration; the partnership continues [00:00]. The Sydney 21K race pack sells at $40.00 ("Fuel your night"): eight packs of Run Fuel Endurance energy gels (3 x 60 ml), Run Hydro+ electrolyte powder (4.3 g), a Run Fuel Endurance energy chew (50 g) and Run Recovery Endurance powder (73 g) (photo 17).

The Nike x SiS After Dark range, "designed for her", laid out for 10K and half marathon: Run Fuel Isotonic gel (22 g single-source carbohydrate; before and during), Run Fuel Endurance gel (40 g dual source; during), Run Fuel Endurance chew (40 g dual source, 1:0.8 glucose to fructose; before and during), Run Hydro+ sugar-free electrolytes (350 mg sodium; before, during and after), Run Recovery (25 g single-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) and Run Recovery Endurance (40 g dual-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) (photo 19).

"The biggest barrier to fueling the female runner is not biological... it is educational"; under-fuelling is cultural; he does not believe in day-of-cycle fuelling messages [00:00]. The closing slide: the barrier "is not likely a biological limitation i.e. their gut or their muscles" but "lack of knowledge and awareness of the guidelines", in "a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent"; fuelling "is less about hormones and tailoring to the menstrual cycle, put simply, it is about fuelling for the work required" (photo 20).

Q&A: nine participants gives 80% power because a 30 g step changes oxidation by 0.3 to 0.4 g a minute [22:54]; women should probably be dosed per kilogram of fat-free mass, but it is hard to measure [23:48]; 60 g was maltodextrin only, 90 and 120 g dual source; dual source is needed above about 90 minutes and lowers oxidation at 60 g [24:34], [25:17].
